## Getting Started


### 1. Early Course Access and Your Tutor

You have been given early access to the course but will not be able to add to the discussion board or upload assignments until your course start date. During this early access time, please use the course only to familiarize yourself with its structure and to download the textbook; do not work ahead and complete any course work yet, as it’s essential to be in contact with your tutor first. As your start date approaches, check your AU portal for an e-letter identifying your tutor. Then, during the first week of the course, monitor your AU email for a personalized welcome message from your tutor. If you do not receive one after the first week, please email your tutor directly. Establishing a working relationship with your tutor and staying in regular contact will be a significant benefit throughout your English 255 course.



## Course Information


### 2. Introduction

Welcome to English 255: Introductory Composition. To pass this course, you must demonstrate the ability to summarize; to use research methods and document sources correctly; to adapt to various writing requirements calling for a range of approaches; and to think and write critically. Developing these skills is the primary reason for taking ENGL 255.

Considering that the vast majority of students rate ENGL 255 highly, we believe the course provides an outstanding learning opportunity. We will continue to seek your recommendations for improvements.

The Digital Reading Room (DRR) is either not currently available or you have Javascript turned off. You can go directly to the DRR by going to http://drr.lib.athabascau.ca

#### Course Learning Outcomes

By the end of this course, you should be able to

1. summarize, quote, and paraphrase
2. use effective research methods and proper citation techniques
3. adapt to various writing requirements that call for a variety of rhetorical modes
4. think and write critically
5. write effective essays that meet first-year university expectations for content, organization, style, mechanics, and grammar

#### Course Outline

- Unit 1: Writing Paragraphs
- Unit 2: Writing a Summary
- Unit 3: Writing an Expository Essay
- Unit 4: Writing an Annotated Bibliography
- Unit 5: Writing a Research Essay
- Unit 6: Writing an Argumentative Essay

#### Course Tutor

Your tutor has excellent academic qualifications and is skilled at and committed to helping you learn at a distance. If at any point in the course you encounter anything that needs clarification, whether it be about course content or how to approach assignments, please do not hesitate to [get in touch with your tutor](http://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=63626). Your tutor is there to help you, and students who keep in regular contact with their tutors are more likely to be successful in their courses than those who do not. Your tutor is also responsible for marking your assignments.

### 4. Evaluation for Credit

To receive [credit](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=62433) for ENGL 255, you must complete and submit all of the assignments and quizzes, and write the final exam. You must achieve a minimum grade of [D (50 percent)](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=58526) on the final exam and an overall grade of at least D (50 percent) for the course.

You will be evaluated on your understanding of the concepts presented in the course and on your ability to apply those concepts. Your final grade in the course will be based on the marks achieved for the following activities.

#### Assignments

Information about the individual assignments can be found in the Assignment Instructions links in the Study Guide, Activities, and Assessments section. Please submit all assignments using the tools provided in the Assessments tab—**do not email your assignments**. If you are unable to submit an assignment, contact your tutor.

Assignments should be completed and submitted in the order presented in the Study Guide. To maximize your learning experience and to reduce the stress on your tutor at certain times of the year, please make sure to submit your assignments as you progress through the course, rather than submitting them all at the same time. This way you will also benefit from your tutor’s feedback, allowing you to achieve the best grade possible.

Use a standard citation style (MLA or APA) consistently and correctly, and carefully proofread your assignments before submitting. Visit the [AU Library’s Guide to Citation Style](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=63597) for access to many excellent citation resources. You may also wish to consult [AU Library’s Guide to the Research Process](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=63996), which contains a step-by-step guide to academic research, as well as information about searching for scholarly materials in AU Library collections.

All assignments (with the exception of the final exam) must be submitted in Microsoft Word (.docx) format. Assignments written in Microsoft Word should use standard font style and size (12-point Times New Roman), have one-inch margins, and be double-spaced. They must be submitted in the drop boxes on the course homepage.

You should not assume that your essays in ENGL 255 will receive the same grades as essays you may have written for other university courses. In ENGL 255, you are assessed on your skill as a critical reader and writer.

#### Marking Scheme

Every assignment you write in ENGL 255 will be evaluated for content, organization, mechanics, grammar, and style. Although all five marking scheme categories are considered for every assignment you write in ENGL 255, some tutors provide a breakdown of grades while others choose a more holistic approach. All tutors are encouraged to use their expertise and learned best practices to grade independent of a standard English 255 rubric. Rest assured that all our tutors are highly experienced experts who will provide a fair assessment.

1. **Content**refers to the following elements:

1. a workable, properly composed thesis
2. an awareness of audience and purpose
3. a clear understanding and complete analysis of the topic
4. a workable topic sentence for each paragraph (stated or implied)
5. a thoughtful presentation of main supporting ideas in each paragraph
6. use of appropriate quotations (where relevant)
7. originality of ideas and expression evidence of critical thinking
8. appropriate evidence of reading and research (where relevant)

2. **Organization**refers to the following elements:

1. a clear, well-placed thesis statement
2. clear, well-placed topic sentences (if stated)
3. a variety of effective transitions to make the writing “flow”
4. an appropriate and logical structure within each paragraph and the essay as a whole
5. maintenance of purpose of the writing
6. an introduction, a developed body, and a conclusion as appropriate within paragraphs and the essay as a whole

3. **Mechanics**refers to the following elements:

1. spelling: correct and consistent
2. punctuation: correct, consistent, and with appropriate variety
3. capitalization: correct and consistent
4. documentation: correct and consistent
5. format: correct and consistent

4. **Grammar**refers to the following elements:

1. sentence formation (clauses and phrases appropriately formed and connected—no sentence fragments, run-on sentences, or comma splices)
2. word order and form
3. verb tense, form, voice (active or passive), and mood (indicative, imperative, subjunctive)
4. subject-verb agreement
5. pronoun case forms and pronoun agreement with antecedent
6. appropriate adjective and adverb forms
7. parallelism
8. appropriate use of modifiers

5. **Style**refers to the following elements:

1. evidence of stylistic control
2. writing at the appropriate language level (informal, general, formal)
3. writing at the appropriate academic level
4. writing appropriate to content, subject, purpose, and audience
5. demonstration of effective tone and appropriate vocabulary
6. effective sentence variety
7. evidence of creativity
8. length and complexity of sentences
9. maintenance of consistent style

Common indicators of stylistic problems include the following:

1. shift of focus
2. monotonous repetition of one or two syntactical patterns
3. change in level or tone
4. pretension (attempt at outward show of ability that appears to be false or inaccurate)
5. use of slang expressions and clichés
6. choppiness (short, unconnected sentences)

### 6. Academic Integrity

Students registered in Athabasca University courses are considered to be responsible scholars and are therefore expected to conform to the highest standards of academic integrity in all written assignments, including examinations. Before you complete your assessment activities, ensure that you have read Athabasca University’s [Student Academic Misconduct Policy](https://www.athabascau.ca/calendar/undergraduate/general-information/legal-notes-and-regulations.html#studentcodeofconductandrighttoappealsregulations). If you have any further questions or concerns about plagiarism, consult with your tutor.

#### Generative AI and Academic Integrity

Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) refers to software programs that can produce written text on nearly any topic. Examples of generative AI include OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google Bard, Microsoft Copilot, and others.
In the context of this course, we strongly discourage the use of generative AI for the purpose of assisting with assignments. Asking an AI to do this work for us would rob us not only of integrity, but of creative experiences and personal growth. We also want you to avoid so-called study websites such as Course Hero, Studocu, and many others, as they are cheating services that put the user at serious risk of academic misconduct. Generative AI can have many legitimate uses, but writing assignments for your coursework is not one of them. To help you achieve your potential in this course, your tutor needs to see your own writing, flaws and all.

If you still make the choice to use generative AI to assist with your work in some way, despite our strong recommendation not to do so, you must discuss your intentions with your tutor in advance and keep them apprised of how you use the software. Your tutor will advise you on whether your intended use of the software is acceptable. Equally important, your tutor may insist on seeing what the AI has generated before you proceed with your first draft. In addition, you must cite the AI as a source, just as you would cite any other source that contributes to the ideas in your written work. For this, you must use the [MLA guidelines for citing generative AI](https://style.mla.org/citing-generative-ai/). Use extreme caution and document your use of the AI diligently at each step. Again, we strongly caution you against having an AI contribute to your work, in part because the AI may have drawn its material from thousands of sources without proper attribution; even if you cite the AI diligently, the human creators of those ideas are not being properly acknowledged.

We know that you work hard to produce your own original assignments, and in order to protect the value of your work and ensure the integrity of the course, we will pursue cases of plagiarism and cheating to the full extent of the [Student Academic Misconduct Policy (PDF)](https://www.athabascau.ca/university-secretariat/_documents/policy/student-academic-misconduct-policy.pdf). The intentional concealment of a source of information is plagiarism, and we do not tolerate plagiarism at AU. **To be clear: submitting an assignment that was written by AI, or that contains ideas supplied by an AI without full and accurate acknowledgement, is plagiarism.**

Tutors in this course may use Turnitin plagiarism detection software. In addition, tutors may use a variety of strategies to detect the use of AI. If your tutor has reasons for concern, you may be directed to compose a new essay on a new topic. This measure exists alongside the tutor’s authority to submit a report to the Academic Integrity Officer for investigation into plagiarism or cheating. As always, the best way to avoid any problems is to discuss your writing process with your tutor and to document your sources with full transparency.

Do you still have questions about the implications of AI for your work? If so, reach out to your tutor, who will be happy to discuss any ideas or concerns you might have.



### 7. The Textbook

We suggest that you first read the section “To the Student: How to Use This Book” in *Read, Think, Write*. Understanding how your textbook works should serve you well as you proceed through ENGL 255.

The reading assignments in the Study Guide refer to specific parts, chapters, and sections of *Read, Think, Write*rather than to specific page numbers. The quickest way to locate certain pages is to make good use of the “Table of Contents” section near the front of the book. The online version book itself has internal links that will facilitate easy navigation to related subjects.

As the preface explains, *Read, Think, Write*has six parts:

#### Part 1: Welcome to University

The first three chapters will familiarize you with university studies by offering exercises and discussion points to help you reflect on your academic skills and be successful in your studies.

#### Part 2: The Writing Process

This part of the textbook will help you regardless of the writing assignment in any academic setting (and well beyond it). It covers the steps writers take to ensure success. You will likely return to it with each assignment—in this course and in others. We suggest that you read all of Part 2.

#### Part 3: Building Paragraphs and Essays

Invariably, good writers are also active readers. Part 3 of *Read, Think, Write*presents an interesting selection of essay models. You should read the introduction to Part 3 as well as the introductions to each of the three sections within Part 3.

#### Part 4: Common Writing Assignments

This part of the textbook is another one that you will likely return to in several of your university courses beyond ENGL 255. It discusses more assignments than one course can cover in the limited time available to complete the readings and the assignments.

#### Part 5: Research and Documentation

Inevitably, your university courses will require you to conduct research and to integrate your findings into your written assignments. We do so in this course. This part of the textbook will help you understand how to do research, why and how you need to document your sources, and how to distinguish a good source from a not-so-good source.

#### Part 6: Writer’s Handbook

This portion of the textbook is a handbook that allows you to easily look up matters related to style, grammar (including solutions for common grammatical errors), and mechanics (punctuation, capitalization, and italicization). If your tutor points out a recurring grammatical or mechanical error, turn to the handbook for help.

Each chapter of *Read, Think, Write* has exercises that reinforce what you read through practice; like many other skills in life, writing improves with practice.



### 8. Final Exam

At the end of your course, you will write a three-hour supervised (invigilated) final exam to ensure that you have achieved the learning outcomes of the course. You may take a dictionary with you (and it may combine English and another language if English is not your first language).

The final exam counts for 20% of your course mark, and you must achieve a mark of 50% or better on the exam to pass the course. If you do not pass the exam the first time, you may write one supplemental exam. See the Athabasca University Undergraduate Calendar for more information on [supplemental exams.](https://www.athabascau.ca/calendar/undergraduate/exams-grades/supplemental-exams.html)

The exam results and your final grade will be available to you approximately five business days after you write it. The exam will not be returned to you, but you will receive a brief note from your tutor with your results. Should you wish to appeal your exam grade, consult [Appeals](https://www.athabascau.ca/calendar/undergraduate/exams-grades/marks-and-grades.html#appeals) in the online Athabasca University Undergraduate Calendar for more information.

#### Exam requirements

This is an [online exam](https://www.athabascau.ca/support-services/exam-services-support/writing-online-exams.html), and it will contain the following four sections:

##### Part A: Essay (50 marks)

Write a 500- to 600-word essay on your choice of five topics. The topics will be general enough to allow you to write based on your personal experience and knowledge. Your essay should demonstrate proficiency in one of the following five modes of organization: process, classification, comparison, cause-effect, or argumentative. Take time to create an outline or a plan and be sure to focus the essay on a clear thesis. The essay should include the following:

- a title
- an introductory paragraph that includes a strong thesis statement
- two or three body paragraphs, each beginning with a topic sentence
- a concluding paragraph that sums up and restates the thesis

Set aside time for both planning and proofreading. The essay will be marked on content, organization, mechanics, grammar, and style.

Part A is worth 50% of the exam mark, so spend approximately 50% of your time (60 to 90 minutes) on it.

**To prepare for Part A,** review **Chapters 12** and **16** in [Read, Think, Write](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=74852). Review your tutor’s feedback on Assignments 3 and 5. Practice writing an essay, from start to finish, within a time limit. Referring to Chapters 16 and 17 of *Read, Think, Write*, choose one of these topics:

- Practice 16.2 (classification essay)
- Practice 16.3 (comparison essay)
- Practice 16.4 (cause-effect essay)
- Practice 16.5 (process essay)
- Practice 17.2 (argumentative essay)

Give yourself 75 minutes to write the practice essay, from planning to proofreading. If you are pressed for time and can’t practice writing a full essay, prepare a thesis and detailed outline instead.

##### Part B: Summary (20 marks)

For Part B, you will read an unfamiliar article (provided with the exam). Then, you will write a one-paragraph summary of that article (approximately 150–200 words in length). Begin the paragraph with the article title, the author’s name, and a restatement of the author’s thesis. Then, follow the steps in “10 Steps to Writing a Successful Summary” (in **Chapter 15** of *Read, Think Write*) to write a summary of the article.

Part B is worth 20% of the exam mark, and you will spend approximately 30 minutes on it.

To prepare for Part B, review Chapter 15 in *Read, Think, Write*, paying particular attention to “10 Steps to Writing an Effective Summary” and “The Dos and Don’ts of Writing a Summary.” Review your tutor’s feedback on Assignment 2.

Practice writing a summary. Choose one of the articles in Unit 2 that you have not already written about. Choose one page of the article to summarize. Give yourself 40 minutes to read the page and to write a summary.

##### Part C: Excerpt Analysis (10 Marks)

For Part C, you will need to be familiar with **one** of the essays listed below. Most likely, you will choose the essay you summarized for Assignment 2, but if you prefer, you may choose another.

- [“How to Write with Style”  by Kurt Vonnegut](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=75524)
- [“I Wrote the Super Queer Novel My Younger Self Needed”](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=75525) by Celia Laskey
- [“Life Is Too Short for Someone Else’s Shame”  by Amanda Leduc](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=75526)
- [“No Place for Self-Pity, No Room for Fear”](https://www.thenation.com/article/archive/no-place-self-pity-no-room-fear/) by Toni Morrison
- [“On Fighting for Space in the Literary World as a Black Canadian Writer”  by Cheryl Thompson](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=75528)
- [“On Keeping a Notebook”  by Joan Didion](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=75529)
- [“Politics and the English Language”  by George Orwell](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=75530)
- [“Shitty First Drafts”  by Anne Lamott](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=75531)
- “Why I Write”  by Joan Didion

  [Digitally transcribed version](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=75532)

  [PDF file of scanned original](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=75533)
- [“Why I Write”](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=75534) by George Orwell
- [“Why I Write Indigenous Sci-Fi”](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=75535) by Drew Hayden Taylor
- [“Write Till You Drop”  by Annie Dillard](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=75536)

On the exam, you will see a list of twelve excerpts, one from each essay listed above. You will choose one excerpt to work with.

You will write a paragraph that a) identifies the essay title and the author, and b) examines the role and significance of the excerpt and how it functions in the article in relation to the author’s thesis. (See Preparing for the Final Examination, below, for more information.)

Part C is worth 10% of the final exam mark, and you will likely spend 20 to 30 minutes on it.

###### Prepare for Part C

For Part C, you will work with **one** of 12 essays. Do not try to memorize all 12 essays. Do not even memorize one! You do not need to read any of the other essays listed for Part C **except**for the one you wish to work with.

Shortly before the exam, review your notes from Learning Activity 5 in Unit 2. Re-read your chosen essay. Memorize the title and author. Read the essay closely, using the active reading strategies you learned in Unit 2. Write out a restatement of the author’s thesis, in your own words. Memorize it. Identify the main supporting points.

To practice for Part C, choose an important sentence from your essay and pretend that it is the excerpt you see on the exam. Determine the role of excerpt:

- Is it the author’s thesis statement?
- Is it a key supporting idea?
- Is it a main argument or a key reason?
- Is it a piece of evidence?
- Is it a supporting detail? If it is a supporting detail, is it a statistic, a fact, an example, an anecdote, etc?
- Is it an analogy or a metaphor?
- Does it appeal to logic or emotion?
- Is it an introduction or a conclusion?
- Does it have any other roles, such as establishing tone?

Give yourself 20 minutes to write a paragraph that 1) identifies the title and author, 2) restates the article’s thesis, and 3) thoroughly explains the role of the excerpt by answering the questions above.

In the first sentence of your paragraph, identify the essay title and the author (“This excerpt is from . . . ). Then, paraphrase the author’s thesis.

The rest of the paragraph should be devoted to identifying the role and significance of the quotation. How does the excerpt relate to the author’s thesis? What is the job of the quotation in supporting the thesis? Which specific words or phrases in the quotation demonstrate its role? In your paragraph, quote them and explain their significance.

##### Part D: Grammar and Mechanics (20 marks)

Part D consists of 20 multiple-choice questions, each containing one of the errors included in “20 Common Errors” document you read in Unit 1. For example, a question might contain a comma splice, a sentence fragment, a semicolon error, a parallelism error, a dangling participle, etc. You do not need to be able to label/name the errors, but you do need to be able to identify a correct or incorrect sentence from a multiple-choice list.

Part D is worth 20% of the exam mark, and it will likely take only 15 to 20 minutes if you have prepared adequately.

To prepare for Part D, review the “[20 Common Errors](/d2l/common/dialogs/quickLink/quickLink.d2l?ou=23965&type=content&rcode=1016B7DC-1AE1-44D6-994A-A790405445BA-156501)” document, and study the examples. All 20 errors will be represented on the exam. Pay particular attention to the errors that your tutor has flagged in your assignments.

#### Extra Notes for a Successful Final Exam

1. You may take a dictionary into the exam, but you may not use any other books or sources.
2. **On exam day, be as rested and relaxed as you can.** Above all, have a good night’s rest and try to relax. This exam should have no surprises. We want to assess your essay-writing, summarizing, and critical thinking skills. We also want to see your ability with grammar and have assurance that the tone and style of your writing matches that of your previous course submissions. We do not expect your writing to be as polished as it might be if you had more time.
3. **Manage the exam.** Look the whole exam over once. This will calm your nerves and prepare you to write.
4. **Remember:** You have a maximum of three hours to complete the exam. Most students use the full three hours. Budget your time accordingly.
5. **Proceed** to Part A and
   - choose the essay topic you would like to write about.
   - answer the following questions for yourself—and based on those answers, make a rough outline for the essay:
   1. Who is my audience?
   2. What is my purpose?
   3. Therefore, what should be my style and type of writing (e.g., personal, expository, persuasive)?
   4. What is my thesis?
   5. What is the topic/topic sentence in each of my three or four body paragraphs?
   6. What sort of supporting detail will I need to mention for each point made in each paragraph?

   Your essay should demonstrate a clear, sufficiently detailed thesis (usually placed at the end of your opening paragraph) and two or three solid body paragraphs of 6 to 12 sentences each. Use good paragraph craft so that each paragraph has focus, support, and a clear, effective relationship to your thesis. **Give yourself 90 minutes for planning and writing your essay.**
6. **Use** your dictionary. Remember that you may bring a dictionary with you, and it may combine English and another language if English is not your first language. Use your dictionary initially just to check the precise meanings of any key words in the essay assignment instructions. Once you reach the essay-revision stage, use your dictionary to check spellings, if you have time.
7. **Manage** your remaining time. Assuming you have used the full 90 minutes to prepare and write Part A, you will have 90 minutes left to complete your exam. We recommend using that time as follows:

- Part A: 90 minutes
- Part B: 40 minutes
- Part C: 20 minutes
- Part D: 20 minutes
- Final Revision: 10 minutes

This timeline is just a recommendation. The important thing is to keep an eye on the clock so you do not spend too much time on any one section.

#### Some final tips

- Do not waste time typing out exam instructions or essay topics. Instead, get straight to your answer.
- While it is a good idea to jot notes or make an outline for your essay on a piece of paper, do not try to write out a complete first draft. If you do, you will likely run out of time and energy in your final draft.
- You will have limited ability to format your answers in the exam software. You do not need to double-space. Instead of indenting, hit the return key twice and leave a blank line to indicate a paragraph break.
- There is no spell-check in the exam software. Leave time to proofread.
- You do not need to provide any in-text citations or bibliographies.

If you get stuck on a grammar question, guess, then move on. You can go back to it later if you have time. Each grammar question is worth only one mark, so do not waste time pondering an individual question. Your time is better spent proofreading your essay.



## Unit 1: Writing Paragraphs


### 9. Unit 1: Writing Paragraphs

![](ENGL255/Content/04_StudyGuideActivitiesAssessments/01_Unit_01/images/U1_1.jpg)

Album quilt possibly made by the members of the Independent Order of Odd Fellows. 1853. Philadelphia Museum of Art. Artstor. Artstor ID# MICO_PHILADELPHIA_103883629. Textiles.

> Composing an effective paragraph requires a method similar to building a house. You may have the finest content, or materials, but if you do not arrange them in the correct order, then the final product will not hold together very well.
>
> —*Read, Think, Write, Chapter 11*



### 10. Learning Objectives

When you have finished Unit 1, you will be able to

- explain how academic writing differs from other genres of writing
- identify the main steps in the writing process
- prewrite effectively to generate a topic suitable for a specific task
- narrow a topic to meet the needs of purpose and audience
- freewrite effectively to generate ideas
- identify the three parts of a well-organized, well-focused paragraph
- write an effective topic sentence
- draft a paragraph that is unified and coherent
- write an effective closing sentence
- adopt a suitable tone for an introductory paragraph
- edit a paragraph to improve style
- proofread to eliminate errors in grammar and mechanics
- format an assignment according to MLA or APA guidelines
- understand the marking standards of ENGL 255



### 11. Introduction

Paragraphs are the core building blocks of any professional or academic essay. All paragraphs need a clear beginning (a topic sentence), middle (sentences of support), and end (closing sentence). Unit 1 gives you practice in writing paragraphs with those components.

Don’t rush through this unit. Be deliberate. Take one step at a time and give every step your best effort, no matter how many times you have to redo your work. You will learn to write effective paragraphs, which will be essential in writing effective essays, and you will learn to employ a writing process for success with any writing task. When faced with a writing task, no effective writer gets it right on the first try. Good writers use a step-by-step process to produce writing that meets the needs of its purpose and its audience.

You will probably have to spend at least two weeks on Unit 1. You will also need to take the time to read the assigned chapters in the course textbook, [Read, Think, Write](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=74852)*.* We will refer to them again in upcoming units, and you will need to turn back to them to write each assignment in ENGL 255.

Here’s how to successfully complete the learning activities in Unit 1:

1. Do all of the required readings in *Read, Think, Write.*The readings will prepare you well for all the assignments in ENGL 255.
2. In the readings*,* dig into the sections that introduce information that is new to you. Complete all the practice activities in each chapter to be certain you understand the concepts.
3. Reading the textbook is not a replacement for reading the Content section in Brightspace. Reading the unit’s instructions and objectives, following the directions when working through the unit’s learning activities, and using the unit’s checklist when finalizing assignments are the most important elements of this and every unit in the course.
4. Move methodically through the Learning Activities in this unit. Do not skip steps even if you think you already know the concepts.

1. #### Understand what academic writing *is* and what it is *for*

   The first step in learning how to write in a way that is appropriate for an academic setting is to understand what academic writing *is* and what its*purpose*is*.*

   ##### Reading Assignment

   > **[Reading]**
   >
   > [Chapter 3: Introduction to Academic Writing](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=74854), in *Read, Think, Write.*
2. #### Become familiar with the writing process

   ##### Reading Assignment

   > **[Reading]**
   >
   > [Introduction to Part 2: The Writing Process](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=74855), in *Read, Think, Write**.*

   While each individual writer’s process varies somewhat, all successful writers use some version of the writing process described in Part 2 of *Read, Think, Write.* You will be expected to use this process throughout ENGL 255, and you will likely want to keep using it afterwards for writing tasks for school and work.
3. #### Learn the requirements for Assignment 1

   For Assignment 1, you will be required to write two separate introductory paragraphs. In the first paragraph, you will **introduce an aspect of yourself**. In the second paragraph, you will introduce an **aspect of your community or culture**. Both paragraphs will be in a single document.

   Your first step is to choose an appropriate topic, one that suits the purpose, the audience, and the assignment requirements (such as length, for example). A topic that is appropriate for an introductory paragraph might not be appropriate for an expository paragraph, so it is essential to know exactly what kind of paragraph to write.

   Complete the learning activities below before you begin Assignment 1.
4. #### Learn prewriting techniques

   Learn about the benefits of prewriting and some of the specific strategies you can use to generate ideas.

   ##### Reading Assignment

   > **[Reading]**
   >
   > [Chapter 4: Prewrite: Generate Ideas for Writing](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=74856), in *Read, Think, Write.*
5. #### Prewrite to generate ideas for a topic for your first opening paragraph

   Use **idea mapping**  to generate possible topics for the first paragraph. Write the prompt “Things I’d Like People to Know About Me” and then follow the instructions in Chapter 4 to generate and write down ideas. Take at least five minutes, and push your thinking beyond the obvious.
6. #### Select a topic

   Which one of your possible topics is the best way to introduce **a particular aspect of yourself**? Get some guidance from the textbook here:

   ##### Reading Assignment

   > **[Reading]**
   >
   > [Chapter 10: Develop an Effective Topic for a Paragraph or an Essay](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=74857), in *Read, Think, Write.*

   Your theme for the introductory paragraph must apply to you. You might focus on athletic or artistic abilities, a role, a goal, your career history, or a trait you value (such as ambition, creativity, compassion). Be creative in making your choice.

   Follow these steps:

   1. Carefully read the idea map you created in Learning Activity 5. Circle the three topics you would most like to write about.
   2. Based on what you have learned in **Chapter 10**, choose **one** topic.
   3. Is this topic narrow enough for a single paragraph? Remember, you’re not telling everything about yourself. Focus on a single aspect of yourself. Seek a narrowed topic, as with this example:
      1. General Topic: My Family Life and Career
      2. Narrower Topic: Skills I Use at Home and Work
      3. Narrowed Topic: Teamwork

      The third topic is narrow enough to be suitable for a short paragraph.

      If your initial topic needs to be narrowed further, use theidea mapping technique you learned about in **Chapter 4** to generate suitable subtopics.
   4. Apply “Checklist 10.1: Developing a Good Topic” to your topic (find this checklist in **Chapter 10** of *Read, Think, Write*). Does your topic meet the textbook’s criteria or does it require more work?
7. #### Generate content

   1. Think about what you will write in the paragraph now that you have a suitable, narrowed-down topic.
   2. Choose a tone and a point of view.

      For Assignment 1, write from the first-person point of view, using the pronouns *I*, *me*, *my*, *we*, *us*, and*our*. The first-person point of view is used to write about one’s own experiences in a conversational tone. Do keep in mind, though, that this is a university assignment, so avoid extremely informal words such as slang, and use correct grammar and mechanics.

      Also, remember that you are writing for a reader who may not be familiar with your profession, your town, or your culture. If your paragraph includes specialized language that is not familiar to a broad audience, define or explain it. If your paragraph includes words from a language other than English, italicize them.
   3. Freewrite to develop ideas

      Refer to the instructions in the “Freewriting” section of **Chapter 4**, and freewrite for at least ten minutes to develop ideas about the topic you chose.
8. #### Develop an effective topic sentence

   Complete the assigned reading and then follow the steps below to create the first sentence of the paragraph, which is your topic sentence.

   ##### Reading Assignment

   > **[Reading]**
   >
   > [Chapter 11: Paragraph Essentials](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=75066), in Read, Think, Write.
   >
   > Learn the key components of an effective paragraph and how to fit those components together

   ##### Video

   > **[Video]**
   >
   > [“Writing Effective Paragraphs.”](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=74858) AU Write Site.
   >
   > Video tutorial.

   1. Develop an effective topic sentence for the paragraph. It should introduce the topic and the controlling idea of the paragraph.
      - Topic Sentence = Topic + Controlling Idea

      The controlling idea should be sufficiently limited in scope (meaning that you can develop it adequately in a paragraph). See the example below. Can you identify the central topic and the controlling idea?

      - One of the characteristics I value most in myself is that I am a team player.
   2. Ensure your topic sentence avoids statements of intent such as *I will be discussing*, *this paragraph will review*, *the following will present*, and so on.
   3. Check your topic sentence against the**“**Five Characteristics of a Good Topic Sentence” in **Chapter 11**. If necessary, revise your topic sentence before moving on.
9. #### Plan the paragraph

   With the topic sentence you wrote in Learning Activity 8 and the freewriting you did in Learning Activity 7, plan the paragraph. Refer to the sections “Supporting Sentences,” “Transitions,” and “Closing Sentences” in **Chapter 11** of *Read, Think, Write*.
10. #### Draft the paragraph

    Read about strategies for drafting and then write the first draft of the paragraph.

    ##### Reading Assignment

    > **[Reading]**
    >
    > [Chapter 6**:** Draft: Develop a Piece of Writing](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=74859), in Read, Think, Write.

    Write a first draft of the paragraph, keeping in mind what you have learned in **Chapter 11** of *Read, Think, Write*. Follow the steps below. The finished paragraph should stand alone as a complete paragraph and should be 150–250 words long.

    1. The first sentence should be the topic sentence you wrote in Learning Activity 8.
    2. Write the body of the paragraph according to the plan you made in Learning Activity 9. Be sure to include at least two main points that support the controlling idea introduced in the topic sentence. Use specific details to bring your paragraph to life.
    3. End your paragraph with a closing sentence that reinforces the controlling idea (without repeating the topic sentence word for word).
    4. Give the paragraph a title that attracts the reader’s attention and introduces the specific topic of the paragraph. For example, “Compassionate Me” would be more interesting than “Self-Introduction.”
11. #### Select a topic for the second paragraph

    Now that the first draft of the paragraph is complete, turn your attention to the second opening paragraph of Assignment 1.

    The second opening paragraph will be about a **specific** **aspect of your culture or community**. For example, you might focus on your cultural background, your family’s Eid or Christmas celebrations, or the benefits of being part of a community you belong to (a community can be geographical or online, work-related or hobby-related, etc.). Please do not restrict yourself to these examples. Think about an aspect of *your* community or culture that matters most to *you*.

    To choose an appropriate topic for the second paragraph, follow these steps:

    1. Use the **brainstorming** technique to generate possible topics for the paragraph. Write the prompt “Communities/Cultures I Belong To” and then follow the instructions in **Chapter 4** to generate and write down ideas. Take at least five minutes and push your thinking beyond the obvious.
    2. Consider which of those topics will be most suitable for the second paragraph for Assignment 1. Circle or highlight the three topics you would most like to write about for this assignment.
    3. Based on what you have learned in **Chapter 10** of *Read, Think, Write,* choose one topic to focus on in the second paragraph
    4. Consider whether this topic is narrow enough for a single paragraph. You can’t write about an entire culture, so consider the following example of narrowing a topic:
       - General Topic: Jewish Culture
       - Narrower Topic: Jewish Family Traditions
       - Narrowed Topic: My Family’s *Shabbat* Dinners

       The first two topics are too broad, but the third is narrow enough to be suitable for a short paragraph. If your topic needs to be narrowed further, use theidea mapping technique.
    5. Assess your topic using “Checklist 10.1: Developing a Good Topic” near the end of **Chapter 10**. Does it meet the criteria or does it require more work?
12. #### Draft the second paragraph

    To develop the second opening paragraph (on an aspect of your community or culture), go through Learning Activities 7, 8, 9, and 10 again—this time focusing on the new topic. Once you have written a draft of the second paragraph (which includes a title, a topic sentence, a well-developed body, and a closing sentence), move on to Learning Activity 13.
13. #### Read sample paragraphs

    Study the structure of the two sample paragraphs below and then check the structure of your own paragraphs. Your *topics* will differ, but the *structure* of your paragraphs should be similar to the structure of each sample. ***Structure*** refers to the position of organizational elements—title, topic sentence, supporting points, and closing sentence—that create a unified, cohesive paragraph.

    Read the two sample paragraphs below. Can you locate and identify the following:

    - the title
    - the topic sentence
    - the main supporting points (how many are there?)
    - the closing sentence
    > **A Team Player**
    >
    >      One of the characteristics I value most in myself is that I am a team player. As part of a recreational volleyball team, I have learned the importance of cooperation. No matter how well I play, I win only when my teammates win, so I work hard to play in a way that allows everyone to succeed. In addition to being a member of a sports team, I also belong to a team of healthcare professionals committed to helping patients manage chronic disabilities. This team consists of nurses (like me), doctors, families, and patients. On this team, I have learned the importance of clear communication and good procedures. I am a conscientious and caring nurse, and the people I work with make me even better at my job. Finally, as a daughter, wife, and mother, I am part of the most important team of all: my family. I am lucky to be part of a big, loving family, and we all have each other’s best interests at heart. Whether it is on a sports team, in a work setting, or at home, being a strong team player requires the same traits of me: cooperation, communication, compassion, and respectfulness. Every day, I am reminded that I am not flying solo through this life, and I am proud to be a member of these many fine teams.
    >
    > **My Family’s*****Shabbat*****Tradition**
    >
    >      Friday night (or *Shabbat*) dinners are a significant way my family maintains its Jewish culture. Shabbat dinner represents the freedom Jewish people now have to express and preserve their traditions, and it is also an occasion to celebrate and unite family. Since the Jews experienced severe oppression in the form of slavery in Egypt and in concentration camps during the Holocaust, celebrating Shabbat dinner openly in a Jewish home truly represents freedom of religious expression. In my family, we uphold the custom of reciting blessings over candles, wine, and bread. Then, we sit down to enjoy a yummy dinner of Jewish favourites like *gefilte* fish, chicken soup, roasted chicken, and noodle *kugel*. In my family, like in many other Jewish families, Friday night dinners are meaningful and momentous.

    Make sure both of your paragraphs contain the structural elements mentioned above and shown in the samples (title, topic sentence, main supporting points, an engaging, non-repetitive concluding statement). If something is missing, revise your paragraphs.

    When you have completed your first drafts, work through the final stages of the writing process to improve and polish both paragraphs.
14. #### Revise the paragraphs to improve the content

    Do not submit the first drafts for Assignment 1. You will likely need to go through one or two more drafts before the assignment is ready for submission.

    Carefully review and revise your work, asking yourself these questions:

    - Does each paragraph have an interesting title?
    - Does each paragraph begin with a topic sentence?
    - Does the topic sentence introduce the topic of the paragraph and the controlling idea?
    - Are there sufficient supporting sentences to support the topic sentence?
    - Is each sentence in the paragraph directly related to the controlling idea? If not, what should be removed or revised?
    - Are the sentences in the right order?
    - Does the paragraph contain enough detail? Does it include specific examples?
    - Are there sufficient transitional words and phrases to achieve coherence?
    - Have I explained any terminology that my reader might not be familiar with?
    - Does the paragraph end with a strong closing sentence that reinforces the controlling idea without being repetitious?
    - Are your paragraphs in a single document that has been correctly formatted according to either MLA or APA standards (see Learning Activity 17 below for links to help you do this)?

    Once you are happy with the content of each paragraph, move on to the last two steps to prepare the assignment for submission.

17. #### Format and proofread your paragraphs

    Now, format and proofread your paragraphs in preparation for submission.First, decide whether you will use MLA style or APA style to format your assignment:

    - MLA style is typically used in English, history, modern languages, and other disciplines.
    - APA style is typically used in social sciences, nursing, education, Indigenous studies, and other disciplines.

    Learn the assignment formatting requirements for your chosen style. The resources at the links below will show you how to format your assignment. Pay particular attention to margins, spacing, indentation, page numbers, and the layout of the first page.

    As you proceed in ENGL 255, you will use more elements of these style guidelines as you begin to incorporate research in your essay, but for Assignment 1, only the *formatting* requirements apply.

    - [MLA General Format](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/mla_style/mla_formatting_and_style_guide/mla_general_format.html)
    - [MLA Guide to Formatting a Paper (PDF)](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/mla_style/mla_formatting_and_style_guide/documents/20180702110400_747-2.pdf)
    - [APA General Format](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/apa_style/apa_formatting_and_style_guide/general_format.html)
    - [APA Guide to Formatting a Paper (PDF)](https://apastyle.apa.org/style-grammar-guidelines/paper-format/student-annotated.pdf)
    > **[Note]**
    >
    > **Note:** Even experienced researchers and writers visit these pages regularly; changes and new source types do appear, and this site is generally up to date.

    ##### Reading Assignment

### 13. Checklist for Assignment 1

After you have read all the required readings and completed all the Learning Activities in Unit 1, use the checklist below to evaluate whether your two introductory paragraphs are ready for submission. If necessary, revise the paragraphs before submitting them for marking.

1. The first page of the assignment is correctly formatted according to the guidelines of [MLA style](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/mla_style/mla_formatting_and_style_guide/mla_sample_paper.html) **or** [APA style](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/apa_style/apa_formatting_and_style_guide/apa_sample_paper.html). Note that MLA requires a particular format for the first page of the assignment, while APA style requires a separate title page.

2. The rest of the assignment is correctly formatted: headers, page numbers, margins, spacing, and alignment are correct, according to the guidelines of [MLA style](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/mla_style/mla_formatting_and_style_guide/mla_general_format.html) **or** [APA style](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/apa_style/apa_formatting_and_style_guide/general_format.html).  I have compared the formatting of my assignment to the sample on Purdue OWL.

3. The entire document is typed in black 12-point Times New Roman font.

4. The entire document is double-spaced. (Apply automatic double-spacing to the document. If you don’t know how to do so, Google “how to double space in Word.” Do **not** hit “Enter/Return” at the end of each line.)

5. Each paragraph is able to stand on its own as a self-sufficient paragraph of 150 to 250 words.

6. Each paragraph focuses on one specific main idea that can be managed in a single paragraph.

7. Each paragraph has a specific, interesting title that introduces the specific topic.

8. Each title is centred (apply automatic centring—do **not** use the space bar), in 12-pt black font, correctly capitalized, with no period at the end. Note, in MLA style, the title should **not** be bolded; in APA style, it **should be** bolded.

9. The first line of each paragraph is indented—to do so, press the Tab key once. Do **not** use the space bar for this! (Both MLA style and APA style require indentation).

10. Each paragraph begins with a topic sentence that introduces the topic and the controlling idea.

11. Each topic sentence avoids announcements, phrases such as “I will talk about,” “This paragraph will be about,” or “My paragraph will introduce.”

12. Each paragraph contains sufficient supporting sentences (at least two) to support the topic sentence and sufficient specific details or examples for each point.

13. All the sentences in the paragraph are directly related to the controlling idea. (If not, which sentences should be removed?)

14. Each paragraph avoids straying into other topics.

15. Each paragraph ends with a closing sentence that reinforces the controlling idea that was introduced in the topic sentence (without repeating the topic sentence word for word) and avoids common phrases such as “in conclusion” or “to conclude.”

16. The paragraphs are written from the first-person point of view in a conversational tone.

17. Specialized terminology is explained, and words from languages other than English are italicized.

18. I have edited the paragraphs for style and for conciseness.

19. I have proofread the paragraphs: grammar and mechanics (spelling, punctuation, and capitalization) are correct.

20. Both paragraphs are saved in the same Microsoft Word file.

## Unit 2: Writing a Summary


### 16. Unit 2: Writing a Summary

![](ENGL255/Content/04_StudyGuideActivitiesAssessments/02_Unit_02/images/U2_1.jpg)

Artist/maker unknown. Log Cabin Quilt (Barn Raising) from New Mexico. c. 1900. Artstor. Artstor ID# ARTSTOR_103_41822001389962. Textiles.

> You already know how to summarize, and you will use that skill as you learn how to write academic summaries.
>
> —Read, Think, Write, Chapter 15



### 17. Learning Objectives

When you have finished Unit 2, you will be able to

- survey a text to identify the topic, structure, and key components
- read actively to comprehend an academic text
- identify the thesis (or main idea) of a reading, whether it is implied or stated clearly
- restate the thesis in your own words
- recognize the central supporting points of a reading
- isolate the details from the supporting points of a reading
- write and organize a summary
- paraphrase effectively
- avoid accidental plagiarism
- demonstrate an understanding of the importance of naming the author as the source of all information



### 18. Introduction

This course encourages you to read, think, and write carefully and critically. To this end, Unit 2 helps you improve one of the most important skills you will have: how to summarize what others have written. In fact, summarization is the beginning of any academic discussion. In this unit, we practice capturing what others have said about a topic *before*we enter the discussion. Doing so well will make our own contributions more valuable.

> **[Note]**
>
> **Note:** Please follow instructions from your tutor, even if they are not the same as those given in the Study Guide.



### 19. Learning Activities

In Assignment 2, you will summarize an essay about writing. However, before we get to how to summarize, we will first examine how to read closely for a specific purpose. Reading for academic purposes is a very different process from reading for pleasure, so follow the steps below to learn how to read academic texts most effectively.

However, and this is **very important**, please **ignore the sample summary in Chapter 15** since the style we prefer is modeled for you below in Learning Activity 9.

8. #### Prepare to write a summary of your chosen essay

   Review “Table 15.1: The Dos and Don’ts of Writing a Summary in **Chapter 15** of *Read, Think, Write*.

9. #### Read a sample summary

   [Summary of Susan McClelland’s “The Lure of the Body Image”](#rss)

   [In the expository essay “The Lure of the Body Image,” Susan McClelland argues that the media’s portrayal of the male body has dangerous consequences for the physical and psychological health of Canadian men.](#rss) The essay begins with the story of one man who is struggling with body image. [Then](#rss), [McClelland](#rss) claims that the “lure of the body image” affects men’s health because the media increasingly portrays the ideal male body as muscular.  [McClelland](#rss) asserts that escalations in steroid use, eating disorders, and plastic surgery are signs that men are becoming increasingly consumed by society’s distorted image of the perfect male body. She  [reports](#rss) that steroid use amongst survey respondents is largely due to the men's desire to modify their appearances. She also [notes](#rss) a rise in eating disorders, specifically bulimia, in men. [Finally](#rss), McClelland mentions increasing demand for plastic surgery from Canadian men. [She](#rss)  provides statistics and two case studies from plastic surgeons to illustrate the growing popularity of cosmetic surgery, including liposuction, among men.  [To conclude](#rss), McClelland cites an expert in physical education who argues that teaching children about positive self-image is key to combatting the negative health effects of the unrealistic images portrayed in the media.

   Hover over the highlighted sections of the sample summary above for tips that you can use in your own summary. Note that the sample demonstrates the following elements that must be incorporated in your summary for Assignment 2, so follow the sample closely to learn the following:

   1. how to write a title for a summary with the author’s full name (spelled correctly) and the title of the essay, which is placed in quotation marks
   2. how to punctuate and capitalize the title of article you’re summarizing
   3. how to compose an opening sentence for a summary with the author’s full name (spelled correctly) and the title of the essay, which is placed in quotation marks
   4. how to summarize a thesis and main supporting points
   5. how to name the author throughout a summary (examples: *Vonnegut begins by*, *he goes on to explain*, *Vonnegut also points out)*
   6. how to use present-tense verbs in a summary
   7. how to use transitional words to connect ideas in a summary
   8. how to write a closing sentence for a summary

10. #### Write a summary of the essay

    Write a summary of the essay you chose for Assignment 2.

    Paying close attention to the seven items listed above (in Learning Activity 9), complete every step in “Ten Steps to Writing a Successful Summary” in **Chapter 15**.

    This tip from *Read, Think, Write*is so important that we repeat it here:

    > Students often find it challenging to summarize a text without copying the author’s words or grammar. To avoid the temptation to copy, **close the article** before writing each sentence of your summary. This will force you to *paraphrase* (i.e., to use your own words), which will help you avoid accidental plagiarism. This strategy also encourages you to focus on main ideas and to ignore details that are not essential in a summary.
    >
    > **Remember:** Do not look at the essay as you write your summary of each section.

    If your summary requires revision, take time to revise it.

11. #### Check for plagiarism

    Review “Avoiding Plagiarism While Summarizing” in **Chapter 15** and closely review your summary, checking for plagiarism. Be careful to avoid AI and/or looking at*any sample summaries that you might find online* (except the one in the course, which you should model your summaries after). **Be aware** that using even a few words from someone else’s work without citing them is committing plagiarism. The penalties for plagiarism are extreme, so revise the summary as necessary to avoid plagiarizing.

12. #### Add a bibliography

    You don’t need in-text citations for your summary paragraph, but since you are using a source, you need to include a bibliography, even though there will be just one entry—the article you summarized. The bibliography in MLA is called Works Cited; in APA, it is called References. Follow these links to samples:

    [MLA, Works Cited Example](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/mla_style/mla_formatting_and_style_guide/mla_works_cited_electronic_sources.html)

    [APA, References Example](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/apa_style/apa_formatting_and_style_guide/reference_list_electronic_sources.html)

    For **MLA**, follow the sample under the heading “**A Page on a Website,**” and for **APA**, follow the sample under the heading “**Webpage or Piece of Online Content.**"

    There are a few exceptions since Didion’s “On Keeping a Notebook,” Lamott’s “Shitty First Drafts,” and Vonnegut’s “How to Write with Style,” are all PDF versions. For these three articles, follow this pattern:

    **For APA**: Author’s last name, Author’s initials. (Year if there is one). Title of the document. URL.

    **For MLA**: Author’s Last Name, Author’s First Name. “Title of Document,” Year if there is one, URL.

    These are the URLs for the above-named articles:

    1. Didion’s “On Keeping a Notebook”: [sanmiguelwritersconference.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/10/406-706-Looking-Back-Moving-Forward-Jessica-Handler.pdf](https://sanmiguelwritersconference.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/10/406-706-Looking-Back-Moving-Forward-Jessica-Handler.pdf)
    2. Lamott’s “Shitty First Drafts”: [wrd.as.uky.edu/sites/default/files/1-Shitty%20First%20Drafts.pdf](https://wrd.as.uky.edu/sites/default/files/1-Shitty%20First%20Drafts.pdf)
    3. Vonnegut’s “How to Write with Style”: [www.bu.edu/clarion/guides/vonnegut-1980.pdf](https://www.bu.edu/clarion/guides/vonnegut-1980.pdf)

I have compared the formatting of the assignment to the sample on the Purdue OWL. (Remember, MLA requires a particular format for the first page of the assignment, while APA style requires a separate title page.)
2. The entire document is double-spaced and typed in black 12-point Times New Roman font.
3. The summary is structured as a single paragraph of 200 to 250 words.
4. The summary is titled like this:

   Summary of Stephen King’s “What Writing Is”
5. The title is centred (apply automatic centring—do **not** use the space bar), in 12-point black font, correctly capitalized, with **no** period at the end. Note, in MLA style, the title should **not** be bolded; in APA style, it **should** be bolded.
6. The title of the article is enclosed in quotation marks in the title and throughout the summary.
7. The first line of the paragraph is indented; to do so, press the Tab key once. Do **not** use the space bar for this! (Both MLA style and APA style require indentation).
8. The first sentence of the summary includes the title of the article (enclosed in quotation marks), the **full name** of the author, and a restatement of the author’s thesis (in my own words).
9. After the first sentence, the paragraph summarizes all of the article’s main ideas, in the same order that they appear in the article, without omitting any main points, and each section of the summary is proportional to the corresponding section of the article.
10. The summary accurately represents the author’s meaning, without changing his or her ideas or misrepresenting them. Please note that all the authors identify as either he/his or she/her.
11. Each sentence of the summary attributes the ideas to the author by using the author’s **last name** or a pronoun (e.g., “King states …,” “According to King …,” or “He writes …”).
12. The summary uses present-tense verbs to introduce the author’s ideas (e.g., “King states” or “He explains”).
13. Most of the summary is paraphrased—there are few, if any, quotations.
14. If the summary includes any quoted words or phrases, they are enclosed in quotation marks.
15. After the summary, either at the bottom of the page (if there is room) or on a page of its own, there is either a Works Cited (MLA) or References (APA) with a correctly formatted entry of the work that was summarized. I carefully read the information in learning activity 12, followed the correct links, and double checked for correctness.
16. The summary does not contain plagiarism. I have double-checked!
17. The summary does not contain any of the following: the student’s thoughts on the topic of the article or on the author’s writing, any evaluation of the content or the writing, the student’s own figures of speech, or information from other sources.
18. The summary is written from the third-person point of view in a neutral, objective, formal tone.
19. I have edited the paragraph for style and conciseness.
20. I have proofread the assignment: grammar and mechanics (spelling, punctuation, capitalization, and format) are correct.
21. The summary is saved as a Microsoft Word file.

## Unit 3: Writing an Essay


### 23. Unit 3: Writing an Essay

![](ENGL255/Content/04_StudyGuideActivitiesAssessments/03_Unit_03/images/U3_1.jpg)

Names Quilt Project. Bill Bell and Paul Harman. n.d. Artstor. Artstor ID# ARTSTOR_103_41822001398336. Textiles.

> An essay is a collection of closely related paragraphs, each with a specific purpose, arranged to convey a central idea.
>
> —*Read, Think, Write, Chapter 12*



### 24. Learning Objectives

When you have completed the activities in Unit 3, you will be able to

- explain what makes an essay an essay
- identify the purpose(s) of an undergraduate student essay
- explain the purpose of an expository essay
- identify the purpose of a process essay
- prewrite to generate ideas for an essay
- choose and narrow a topic that is suitable for a process essay
- demonstrate an awareness of audience by choosing a topic that is interesting to a general reader
- develop an effective thesis statement for a process essay
- develop an outline for an essay
- write an effective introductory paragraph
- use chronological order to explain a process
- write an effective concluding paragraph
- combine the elements above to write an effective expository process essay that is logically organized
- revise an essay to improve coherence and unity
- edit an essay to improve style
- write fluently, demonstrating an awareness of purpose
- proofread to eliminate grammatical and mechanical errors
- format an essay according to the guidelines of MLA or APA style
- write in a style that is suitable for a general audience (style includes tone, diction, and level of formality)



### 25. Introduction

Now that you have had a chance to refresh your writing skills, it is time to use them as you write an essay.

The undergraduate student essay is one of the most important types of academic writing that you will be expected to produce in university, particularly if you are studying the humanities or the social sciences.

The undergraduate student essay is a unique subgenre of academic writing. It is not quite like a textbook, not quite like a scholarly journal article, and not quite like a report. It has a specific purpose and particular conventions.

At the end of Unit 3, you will be required to write an expository essay of 800-1000 words. To prepare you to write this essay and other essays required in ENGL 255 and beyond, Unit 3 provides a foundation in essay writing.

Establishing this foundation takes some work. Like Unit 1, Unit 3 requires you to read several chapters in *Read, Think, Write*in order to learn the essentials of essay writing. We recommend that you devote at least two weeks to completing the Unit 3 Learning Activities. You will need that time to do the required readings and learn the steps in the process of writing a successful essay.

Think of this time as an investment that will set you up for success in not only Assignment 3, but also Assignments 5 and 6 and all the essays you will write in your university courses in the future.

> **[Note]**
>
> **Note:** Do not rush ahead to complete Assignment 3 immediately. Instead, work carefully and methodically through the Learning Activities. Take time now to establish a foundation that will make you a better writer of essays.

> **[Note]**
>
> **Note:** Please follow instructions from your tutor, even if they are not the same as those given in the Study Guide.

2. #### Choose an essay topic

   The first step in writing a successful essay is to choose an appropriate topic that suits the purpose, the audience, and the assignment requirements (including length, for example).

   A topic that is appropriate for an expository essay might not be appropriate for an argumentative essay, so it is essential to know exactly what kind of essay you are expected to write.

   For Assignment 3, you will write an **expository process essay**: an essay that explains the steps or stages of a process. Your task is to describe **how to complete a particular process** to **achieve a particular goal.**

   To choose an appropriate topic for Assignment 3, first you must understand the criteria, as follows:

   1. the process has a specific goal or result
   2. the process requires specific steps in a specific order
   3. the process is interesting to a general audience
   4. the process will not require technical or specialized jargon
   5. you already know how to do this process well, so **no research** is required
   6. you can explain the process so clearly that a reader who is unfamiliar with the process could complete it based on your instruction

   Once you are clear on the criteria, follow these steps:

   1. Use the brainstorming technique that you learned about in Unit 1 to generate possible topics. On a piece of paper, create a list titled “Things I Know How to Do.” Jot down ten or fifteen things that you know how to do. Give yourself at least five minutes to create this list and push yourself to think beyond the obvious. (For a refresher on brainstorming, review **Chapter 4**: Prewrite: Generate Ideas for Writing, which was required reading in Unit 1).
   2. Now that you have generated some potential topics, consider which of those topics will be most suitable for your essay. You might want to take a moment to review **Chapter 10**: Develop an Effective Topic for a Paragraph or an Essay, which was required reading in Unit 1, to help you determine which of the topics is most likely to be successful. Then, review your brainstorming list. Circle the top three topics: the three topics you would most like to write about for this assignment.
   3. Consider your audience. As we already mentioned, your topic must be interesting to a general audience, an audience of educated adults who are *not* familiar with your career or your field of study. To ensure you are carefully considering your audience, ask these questions:
      - Would a general audience be *interested* in this process?
      - Might a general reader *want* to achieve the goal?
      - Would a general reader be *able* to understand and follow the steps to achieve the goal? If you can’t answer “yes” to the three questions, reconsider your topic.
        > **[Note]**
        >
        > **Remember:** To consider the needs of a general audience, imagine this: In the waiting room of a doctor’s office, a patient (an average Canadian) is browsing a stack of magazines and comes across the title of your essay on the cover of one issue. Would this average reader be interested in picking up the magazine and reading about this process?
   4. After thinking about it for a few hours, go back to your top three list and choose **one** topic you will write about in Assignment 3. Make sure it meets the criteria for an effective topic, as described in **Chapter** **10** and above in Learning Activity 2. Email your tutor with your topic suggestion since approval of your topic choice is required.

   ##### Extra notes on choosing your topic

   Since this essay will be based on your experience, and because you have unique experiences, skills, and abilities, your topic will be unique to you. Further, since no research is permitted for this assignment, you must choose a topic that you are entirely familiar and comfortable with. If you would need to look up information about a process, choose another topic.

   You might be tempted to write about a specialized process you perform at work, but this would not be appropriate for a general audience. You might also be tempted to choose a topic that is too mundane or too simple, such as how to cook spaghetti, which wouldn’t engage most readers. Similarly, avoid writing about well-known or overly broad processes such as how to maintain a skincare routine or follow a workout plan—these topics are often well known and lack the originality needed to hold your audience’s interest. Keep your reader in mind as you choose a topic, aiming for something original, insightful, and accessible. Ideally, choose a process you’ve personally developed or refined—one that your experience allows you to explain clearly and meaningfully to others, one that includes your own perspective and judgment on how to best undertake the process. The more personal and specific your connection to the process, the more compelling your essay will be. To confirm you're on the right path, email your tutor with the following two items:

   **One sentence** stating the topic you’ve chosen for your process essay.
   **One sentence** explaining how your personal experience qualifies you to write engagingly and insightfully about this process.

   The process that you describe must be undertaken for a specific goal. In other words, there must be a *reason* *or purpose* for undertaking the process.

   > **[Note]**
   >
   > **Remember:** The essay must be based on your own experience and knowledge. Do not choose a topic that would require you to conduct research.
3. #### Identify the steps in the process

   Follow these steps to develop content for the essay:

If not, take the time to go back to Step 2 to find a more suitable topic. **Please ignore the point in Chapter 16 about cake baking since the instructions in this unit state that recipe topics are not permitted.
