10. #### Write the introductory and concluding paragraphs

    After writing the body of the essay, you know what your thesis is and what your essay has to say. Next, add the finishing touches: the introductory (first) paragraph and the concluding (last) paragraph—which will frame the content of your essay. Some of you may prefer to write the introduction before you begin the body of your essay, and this is perfectly okay, but make sure to revisit it and refine it as necessary once you have written the body of your essay.

    1. Write the introductory paragraph and the concluding paragraph for your essay. You might want to review **Chapter 14:** “Essay Essentials: Introductory and Concluding Paragraphs”(required reading in Unit 3).
    2. Give your essay an engaging title, referring to the tips for writing an effective essay title in **Chapter 14**.
    3. Remember that there are two approaches to the concluding paragraph. The first emphasizes the thesis and very briefly sums up the main points without repeating the thesis statement word for word (this is often referred to as an exhaustive conclusion). The second is an emphatic concluding paragraph, one that reinforces the thesis without repeating it and **does not** sum up the main points. Instead, this kind of conclusion might offer an evaluation or discuss implications, and so on. For a better understanding, view this information from [Harvard University’s Writing Centre](https://writingcenter.fas.harvard.edu/conclusions). Then, before making a decision on whether to use an exhaustive or emphatic conclusion, **please** reach out to your tutor regarding a preference. No matter what, remember that this is your final opportunity to impress your reader and to emphasize the significance of your discussion.
    4. Note that this paragraph is **not** labeled with the heading, “Conclusion,” nor should there be any other headings throughout your essay.

1. The assignment is correctly formatted: headers, page numbers, margins, spacing, font, indentation, and alignment are correct, according to the guidelines of [MLA style](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/mla_style/mla_formatting_and_style_guide/mla_general_format.html) **or** [APA style](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/apa_style/apa_formatting_and_style_guide/general_format.html). I have compared the formatting of my assignment to the sample on *Purdue OWL.*
2. The assignment is structured as an essay of 1,000 – 1,200 words (excluding the list of sources).
3. The topic of the essay has been supplied by (or approved by) my tutor. The topic has been appropriately narrowed and is suitable for the mode of organization.
4. The essay has an interesting title that is correctly formatted.
5. The introductory paragraph effectively introduces the topic and suggests the mode of organization. This paragraph is not labeled with the heading “Introduction.”
6. The thesis/road map is clearly expressed in the last sentence of the first paragraph, which introduces the topic, the argument, and the main supporting ideas.
7. The thesis statement/road map does not include announcements such as “I will examine,” “This essay will explain,” or “This essay aims to,” “this essay will contrast,” “what follows classifies,” and so on.
8. The body paragraphs are arranged in a way that is consistent with mode or organization, in the most logical order to prove the thesis.
9. Each body paragraph is substantial and focuses on one distinct main idea that supports the thesis. The body paragraphs are **not** preceded by headings.
10. Each body paragraph begins with a topic sentence, includes at least two supporting points, and ends with a closing sentence.
11. The topic sentences and closing sentences do not contain quotations or citations. (There are some exceptions, but usually topic sentences and closing sentences should contain your own ideas expressed in your own words).
12. Each body paragraph contains relevant information from research that effectively supports the main idea of the paragraph and—by extension—the thesis.
13. The essay includes direct quotations, not just paraphrases.
14. Each piece of information from research is introduced and integrated effectively.
15. The essay contains transitional words that emphasize the mode of organization.
16. Noting there are two approaches to conclusions,
    1. according to my tutor’s advice, the concluding paragraph emphasizes the thesis and very briefly sums up the main points, without repeating the thesis statement word for word (exhaustive).
    2. according to my tutor’s advice, the concluding paragraph is suggestive, so it reinforces the thesis without repeating it and **does not** sum up the main points. Rather, it evaluates, discusses implications, calls for action, provides a warning or prediction, or something similar (suggestive).
    3. The concluding paragraph is not labeled with the heading “Conclusion,” nor does any other section of the essay begin with a heading.
17. The essay contains information from no less than four and **no more** than six research sources.
18. Every research source is reputable, reliable, and relevant.
19. At least three of the sources are from peer-reviewed scholarly journals.
20. There is a citation in each sentence that contains information from research sources. Each citation, whether formatted in MLA or APA, contains a page number when one is available.
21. Each citation is correctly formatted and matches the corresponding entry on the list of sources. Remember: the first word of the citation must match the first word of the corresponding entry.
22. The essay does not contain plagiarism—I have double-checked!
23. The list of sources is titled Works Cited (MLA style) or **References** (APA style).
24. The list of sources includes all the sources used in the essay, and each entry is formatted correctly. I have checked the format of each bibliographic entry against an [MLA sample](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/mla_style/mla_formatting_and_style_guide/mla_works_cited_page_basic_format.html) or an [APA sample](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/apa_style/apa_formatting_and_style_guide/reference_list_basic_rules.html).
25. I have revised the essay to improve coherence and unity.
26. I have edited the essay for style and clarity.
27. I have consistently maintained the third-person point of view throughout the essay.
28. I have proofread the assignment: grammar and mechanics (spelling, punctuation, capitalization, and format) are correct.
29. The essay is saved as a Microsoft Word file, and the articles are saved in PDF format. I have named each article with the last name of the first author.

## Unit 6: Writing an Argumentative Essay


### 45. Unit 6: Writing an Argumentative Essay

![](ENGL255/Content/04_StudyGuideActivitiesAssessments/06_Unit_06/images/U6_1.jpg)

Powers, Harriet. Pictorial Quilt. 1895–98, Museum of Fine Arts, Boston. Artstor. Artstor ID# AMICO_BOSTON_103839783. Textiles.

> Acknowledging our biases, seeing issues from unfamiliar points of view, and properly applying the tools of reason may be the greatest task we face in college or university as well as life.
>
> —from *Acting on Words* by David Brundage and Michael Lahey, p. 38



### 46. Learning Objectives

When you have finished Unit 6, you will be able to

- identify the key features of argumentative writing, including a strong, clear expression of opinion and a well-defined line of reasoning
- define the classical argumentative appeals of pathos, logos, and ethos
- consider the relationship between the topic, the reader, and the audience
- identify several rhetorical devices
- identify logical fallacies—and how to avoid them
- explain the various models of argumentation and design an argumentative essay based on one of these approaches
- locate and assess sources relevant to your topic choice
- conduct scholarly research to help you understand both sides of a debate and to develop a logical, reasonable, evidence-based stance
- plan an argument with an appropriate balance of pathos, logos, and ethos
- predict objections and choose the most effective evidence, writing devices, word choices, and style to enhance your argument
- balance your own argument with a conscientious consideration of opposing views (rebuttal)
- identify and avoid logical fallacies
- integrate quotations, use in-text citations, and create a Works Cited or References page



### 47. Introduction

In defense of free speech, the seventeenth-century English poet John Milton wrote, “Give me the liberty to know, to utter, and to argue freely according to conscience, above all liberties.” Many of us would agree, and for this reason we should be conscious of our responsibility to uphold this freedom and learn how to argue effectively. The first step in our learning is to recognize that we are surrounded by arguments. On an average day, we might notice a bumper sticker advocating a political position, a bus trumpeting the advantages of recycling, and a billboard advertising a cosmetic product. We might witness protesters holding up placards, a menu promoting a particular beverage or food item, a television commercial selling a car, and, of course, the all-too-familiar slogan “Like us on Facebook.” All of these are arguments. In fact, composition experts Andrea A. Lunsford, John J. Ruszkiewicz, and Keith Walters assert that *everything*is an argument.

Argument is an effort to persuade readers to do one or more of the following:

- accept a point of view
- make a decision
- pursue a course of action

This does not necessarily mean that there is a right or a wrong answer or that every argument results in a winner or a loser. Some people seem immune to views other than their own, but a carefully reasoned, thoughtfully strategized argument can be powerful, even to readers who are clearly opposed to it.

In Unit 6, you will explore the tools of argumentation, which include summarizing what others have said, showing respect for all points of view, conducting scholarly research to find evidence for both positions in a debate, creating a logical and evidence-based argument using one of several argumentative strategies, and learning the value of rebuttal.

   For Assignment 6, you will be required to write an argumentative essay. The four assigned sections from **Chapter 17** will help you prepare.

   As Lunsford et al. suggest, *all* writing contains an argument to some extent or another, and you will find that the information in **Chapter 17** will help you to write an essay in any discipline.

   - Logical fallacies are errors in reasoning that negatively impact the quality of an argument. Try as many as you like of these interactive online logical fallacies quizzes, and feel free to browse for more online:
   - [“Can You Spot the Fallacy?”](https://www.funtrivia.com/html5/index.cfm?qid=281476) quiz by Fun Trivia
   - [“More Fallacies Quiz II”](https://highered.mheducation.com/sites/007312625x/student_view0/chapter6/more_fallacies_quiz_ii.html) from the website for the textbook *Critical Thinking*(8th ed.) by Brooke Moore and Richard Parker
   > **[Note]**
   >
   > **Optional:** If you think you would benefit from a little more information about persuasion and argumentation before starting work on your essay, please make use of these resources:
   >
   > Watch [“Opinion Essay or Persuasive Essay”](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DqwzYoThUpg)  on *YouTube*.
   >
   > Read [“Arguments on an Essay in Literature”](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/subject_specific_writing/writing_in_literature/writing_in_literature_detailed_discussion/building_an_argument.html)  on the *Purdue OWL*(be sure to read all four topics under “Other OWL Resources”).
3. #### Choose an essay topic for Assignment 6

   ##### Reading Assignment

   > **[Reading]**
   >
   > [Chapter 17: Argumentative Essay,](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=75271) in *Read, Write, Think.*

   For Assignment 6, you will write a 1,000- to 1,200-word argumentative essay based on information from research.

   1. Carefully review the list of topics you received from your tutor.
   2. Begin to narrow down the choices, focusing on topics you are interested in.
   3. Do some initial prewriting on two or three of the topics to stimulate your thinking and generate ideas. Refer to **Chapter 4** of*Read, Think, Write* as needed.
   4. After thinking about it for at least a couple of days, finalize your choice of topic.
4. #### Narrow the topic

   The general topic you chose in Learning Activity 3 is likely too broad to manage in a four-page essay. It is essential to narrow the topic to one that is suitable for a short essay. Follow these steps to narrow the topic.

   1. Create an idea map to help you narrow the topic. Write your general topic in the centre of the map and spend at least five minutes creating a map and gradually coming up with more specific subtopics. Refer to the section [“Idea Mapping”](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=75545) in **Chapter 4** of *Read*,*Think*,*Write* as needed.
   2. Now that you have generated some potential topics, consider which of those topics will be most suitable for your essay. Choose one.
   3. Referring to **Chapter 17** of *Read, Think, Write*, consider whether your chosen topic is specific, singular, significant, and supportable. If not, revise the topic.
   4. A good topic for an argumentative essay is a debate or question that has reasonable arguments on both sides. Check that your topic meets this criterion.
5. #### Consider your essay’s purpose and audience

   Referring to “How to Write an Argumentative Essay” in **Chapter 17** of *Read, Think, Write,*jot down a few notes about your audience and your purpose in writing the essay.
6. #### Conduct Research

   If it has been some time since you completed Assignment 4, take some time to review **Chapter 20:** “Research Sources: Finding and Selecting Relevant, Reliable Sources” in *Read, Think, Write*.

   With your narrowed topic and your purpose in mind, begin to conduct research in order to collect sufficient information for your essay. Use reliable sources: scholarly articles, written by experts, found in academic journals.

   1. Visit the [AU Library](http://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=58386) databases to find relevant, recent academic articles. If you need help, [make an appointment](https://www.athabascau.ca/library/get-library-support/requesting-research-assistance/index.html) with a reference librarian, who will be happy to help you find articles on your specific topic.

      When you search through the library, you are searching through EBSCOhost, which is the research platform the AU library uses. Through this platform, you should use the date limiters they provide to ensure your search results are as current as possible.

      As we mentioned in Units 4 and 5, unfortunately, the AU library has been experiencing some technical issues, and although a repair is in the works, you may run into trouble accessing the AU library’s databases. In that case, conduct an online Google Scholar search to find scholarly resources that are open source, which means they are available for free. If you have access to another university library, please feel free to use it instead of the AU library. Ensure you download any articles you find in PDF.

      If you do use a university library, be aware that EBSCOhost is **not** a database. If you are using MLA formatting for your Works Cited page, and if you use a university library to gain access to articles, you'll need to include the database title, and it will be listed on the result list page under the title of the article you located, along with other bibliographic information. If you use open-source articles, there won’t be databases to list.
   2. Choose**four to** **six sources** to base your essay on. Ensure each source is current (the last 3-5 years), reputable and reliable. Although we prefer that all your sources are scholarly articles, **at least three of these sources must be peer-reviewed journal articles**accessed through the AU Library databases (or the databases of another university library). Although we prefer that all your sources are scholarly articles, at least three of the sources must be peer-reviewed journal articles accessed through the AU library databases, the databases of another university library, or a Google Scholar search for open-source materials. Make sure to download and save each journal article in PDF.
   3. Using the active reading and notetaking skills introduced in **Chapter 2** and **Chapter 20** of *Read, Think, Write*, carefully read the articles and use the highlighting tool to identify information that will be useful for your essay. Take careful notes and be sure to keep track of material you have paraphrased and material you have quoted.
   4. Record the bibliographic information for each article.
   > **[Note]**
   >
   > **Note:** As you were advised in Unit 5, do not rely on a Google search to locate scholarly articles. Access to most scholarly articles requires a subscription, which the AU Library has paid so that you can access a wide range of periodicals.
   >
   > As we’ve mentioned in previous units, avoid relying on a regular Google search to locate peer-reviewed articles because you will see AI output before anything else. Although this may be a good place to start when first learning about a topic, the validity of the information in these AI summaries is often questionable. Always move onward in your search by conducting an online Google Scholar search to find scholarly resources that are open source and available in PDF.
7. #### Generate ideas for writing

   Do some prewriting to brainstorm what you will write in your essay, so it is at the forefront of your mind. This is important because the research you include will support, not replace, what you have to say.

   1. Referring to Chapter 4 of *Read, Think, Write* as needed, brainstorm by freewriting about your topic. Give yourself at least 10 minutes to generate ideas and push yourself to think beyond the obvious.
   2. Create an argumentation scheme like the one in “Figure 17.3” in *Read, Think, Write*.
8. #### Develop a working thesis/road map statement

   Develop a thesis that will guide your essay.

   1. Review the section “Develop a Thesis” in **Chapter 17**.
   2. [Interactive Quiz](/d2l/common/dialogs/quickLink/quickLink.d2l?ou=23965&type=quiz&rcode=fbcedb3c945048f09b0486aa-8) to learn how to identify an effective thesis statement for an argumentative essay.
   3. Review your notes from Learning Activity 5 and Learning Activity 6.
   4. To develop the thesis, you might find it helpful to first pose a *specific question* about your topic. (For example, “Should Canada legalize the use of psilocybin for the treatment of mental illness? Yes or no?”). An ideal question could be answered with both “yes” and “no,” with rational, convincing reasons on both sides. This question probably won't be explicitly stated in your essay, but forming the question will help you to determine your stance or position on the topic.
   5. Thinking about the evidence you found in your research, answer the question you generated above: “yes” **or** “no”? This will help you identify your essay’s *position* on the topic. Remember, the position must be based on *evidence* from research. It should not be based on your own *opinions*.
   6. Thinking about the evidence you found in your research, identify two to four main *claims*that support that position. This will form your road map.
   7. Write a one-sentence thesis/road map statement that includes the topic, the position, and the claims.
   8. Review the section “Reconsider Your Thesis” in **Chapter 20** of *Read, Think, Write*. If necessary, revise your thesis/road map.
9. #### Plan the essay

   With your thesis/road map statement in front of you, plan the organization of the essay. An argumentative essay requires a special structure, and there are several possible structures available. Below are two effective patterns you can follow.

   1. Carefully study the structure of Pattern A and Pattern B. What are the similarities between the two? What are the differences?

      ##### Pattern A

      In some cases, you may wish to clear away the opposition’s claims before you present the arguments for your side. If so, try Pattern A, which allows you to address all the counter-arguments first and then focus the rest of the essay on arguments in favour of your stance.

      **Thesis**

      **Body paragraph 1:** refute your opposition’s points if you deem it necessary to do so. If a full paragraph of refutation seems unnecessary, you can instead make space within each body paragraph to foresee and address any possible objections to the points you present in that paragraph. Be mindful that the only reason you should rebut or refute a counter-argument is to further promote your thesis.

      **Body paragraph 2:**present your first point and its supporting evidence

      **Body paragraph 3:** present your second point and its supporting evidence

      **Body paragraph 4:**present your third point and its supporting evidence

      **Conclusion**

      ##### Pattern B

      In some cases, you may want to use your opposition’s claims to build your own argument. If so, try Pattern B, in which each body paragraph begins with a brief mention of the opposition’s views, and then the rest of the paragraph refutes that view and builds support for your thesis.

      **Thesis**

      **Body paragraph 1:** present a point of opposition and then use supporting evidence to refute it

      **Body paragraph 2:** present a second point of opposition and then use supporting evidence to refute it

      **Body paragraph 3:** present a third point of opposition and then use supporting evidence to refute it

      **Conclusion**
   2. Carefully examine these sections of **Chapter 17** of *Read, Think, Write*:
   - Template for Outline
   - Sample Outline3. Think carefully about whether Pattern A or Pattern B is a better choice for your essay. Which will develop your argument most effectively? Choose a pattern to follow.
   4. Based on the pattern you have chosen, create a topic outline for your essay that includes a well-developed thesis statement.
   5. **Recommended:** Email your thesis statement and a very brief point-form outline to your tutor so that you can receive feedback before proceeding.
10. #### Write the first draft of the essay

    You will probably write the first draft of the essay concurrently with Learning Activity 9 (above).  You may also find you need to return to Learning Activity 6 to conduct more research.

    1. Determine the tone, style, and point of view. Refer to the section “Establish Tone and Style” in **Chapter 17** of *Read, Think, Write*.
    2. Use a relatively formal tone in a research-based argumentative essay. Use the third-person point of view, using the pronouns *he*,*she*,*one*,*it*, and *they*. Unless it is necessary for a very particular purpose, do not use the second-person point of view (*you*,*your)* or the first-person point of view (*I*,*me*,*my)*. However, the first-person plural “we, our, us” is sometimes used to create inclusivity in argumentative writing. If you wish to use this rhetorical tool, check with your tutor first. To avoid grammatical pronoun agreement errors, make plural nouns your first choice (for example, write *people* instead of *a person,* or *seabirds* instead of *a seabird*).
       > **[Note]**
       >
       > **Remember:** You are writing for a general audience. This means that you must use diction that an average, non-specialist person can understand. If specialized terminology is required, explain it, and cite a source.
    3. Write a first draft of the body of the essay. Refer to your outline to guide your writing. The body paragraphs should thoroughly develop the claims in order to defend the position set out in the thesis statement. The more thorough and detailed, the better. Do not leave any stone unturned. Include specific, logical examples, and integrate information (both quotations and paraphrases) from your research.If it has been some time since you read **Chapter 11**: “Paragraph Essentials”(an assigned reading in Unit 1), take time to review it now. You will need to apply standard paragraph format to the body paragraphs of your essay.
    4. Make sure the essay addresses opposing arguments. To effectively argue for your side, you need to acknowledge and refute arguments on the opposite side of the debate. This is called concession-refutation. There are several ways to approach this based on whether you are following Pattern A or Pattern B, and based on what your approach to the topic requires. When writing persuasively, assume that your audience opposes your thesis. Then, as you write, aim to foresee any possible objections the opposition might have to your argument, and address those objections as necessary. This might be as simple as a sentence in your introduction or a sentence or two within the body paragraphs. Depending on the debate, a paragraph after your introduction or before your conclusion might be necessary. Be mindful that the only reason to address opposing arguments is to rebut or refute them in order to further promote your thesis.
11. #### Incorporate Research

    In a research-based essay, information from research is included to support your thesis and your claims. In previous steps, you chose relevant reputable research on this topic. Now it is time to select information from those sources and integrate the research into the body paragraphs of your essay.

    Each body paragraph should contain several pieces of research that support a main point. This research should come from scholarly journals—not blogs, editorials, corporations, or other unreliable sources. Choose reputable scholarly articles written by experts.

    The central argument of this essay must be based on objective facts. Do not write about your own experiences or feelings. While your opinion will be implied in your thesis, do not explicitly write about your opinions. (Do not use phrases such as “I think …” or “I believe …”).

    You may find it helpful to refer to the following chapters in [*Read, Think, Write*](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=74852), which were assigned readings in Units 1 and 3:

    Review **Chapter 20**, “Thinking Critically About Information from Research”

    Review **Chapter 24**: Integrating Research: Paraphrasing and Quoting

    Review **Chapter 25**: Documentation: Plagiarism, Citations, and the List of Sources

    1. Review AU’s [policy on plagiarism and academic misconduct](http://calendar.athabascau.ca/undergrad/current/student-code/index.php#acad_misconduct).
    2. Choose information from research that supports your main points and your thesis.
    3. Think carefully about when to paraphrase and when to quote based on what you learned in **Chapter 24** of *Read*, *Think*, *Write*.
    4. Select valuable direct quotations. **These are a requirement**, not an option. Every essay is different, so the number of quotations will vary, but consider incorporating one quotation into each substantial body paragraph.
    5. Ensure you have followed the four steps for borrowing researched material (whether paraphrasing or quoting):
       1. position the quotations in your essay according to either MLA or APA rules
       2. integrate/blend/introduce the source (using a variety of the three methods). **Do not “drop” quotations**
       3. credit the source in a parenthetical citation. Stop and check that you have cited a source in every sentence that contains information from research, whether it is paraphrased or quoted. Remember, if a source is paginated, provide the page number. For English 255, this is required in both MLA and APA. Open the PDF version of an article (if available) so you can properly identify the original page numbers.
       4. discuss and relate the research to your main points to avoid hit and run quotations, referred to in the Unit 5, Activity 8 lectures.
          > **[Note]**
          >
          > **Note**: If necessary, refer back to Unit 5, Learning Activities8g and 9, and review the lectures (either MLA or APA).
12. #### Write the introductory and concluding paragraphs

    After writing the body of the essay, you know what your central argument is and what the key claims are. Now add the finishing touches: the introductory (first) paragraph and the concluding (last) paragraph will frame the content of your essay.

    Some of you may prefer to write your introduction before you begin the essay, and this is perfectly okay, but make sure to revisit it and refine it as necessary once you have written the body of your essay.

    1. Write the essay’s introductory paragraph. The introductory paragraph should begin with a hook and a statement about the controversy/issue/debate. Briefly explain the relevance of the issue (i.e., show that the debate exists and matters), share the opposition’s main claim, and then transition into your thesis/road map sentence. The final sentence of the introductory paragraph will state your essay’s position and the main claims (reasons).
    2. Write the concluding paragraph. Remember that there are two approaches. One consists of briefly summarizing the main claims and reinforcing the thesis (exhaustive conclusion). The second approach is more suggestive (emphatic conclusion) in that the thesis is reinforced, but the main points are **not** summarized, particularly in a short essay like this one. **Check with your tutor to find out the preference**. Remember that this is your final opportunity to impress your reader and to emphasize the significance of this debate.
    3. Write an engaging title that names the issue/debate and implies the essay’s position on that topic. Refer to the section "Write an Effective Essay Title" in **Chapter 14** of *Read, Think, Write,* and complete Checklist 14.1.
13. #### Review the logic of your argument.

    1. Complete “Checklist 17.1: Using Sound Arguments” in **Chapter 17** of*Read, Think, Write*.
    2. Review the section “Revise and Edit the Essay”at the end of Chapter 17, and check to make sure your essay has **avoided** these pitfalls:
       1. summarizing the debate rather than arguing for one side
       2. losing perspective
       3. exaggerating
       4. relying on logical fallacies
       5. lacking sufficient evidence from reputable scholarly sources
       6. not considering or addressing opposing arguments
       7. writing an opinion paper or a rant rather than a research essay
    3. Now that the first draft of your essay is complete, revise the content of your essay. You might want to review **Chapter 7**: “Revise: Improve *What* You’ve Written”(which was required reading in Unit 3).
    4. Referring to the first draft of your essay, complete “Checklist 7.2: Revise for Coherence.”
    5. Complete“Checklist 7.3: Peer Review: Revising for Organization, Coherence, and Unity.”
    6. Revise your essay as needed.
    7. If possible, work with a peer or a friend to complete “Practice 7.7”so that you can receive helpful feedback on your writing; then, revise again.

    Consider using the Write Site’s [coaching support](http://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=63614). Your ENGL 255 tutor is not expected or encouraged to review your drafts, but reviewing drafts is one of the mandates of the Write Site.

    > **[Note]**
    >
    > **Note:** Do not submit the first draft of your essay. You will likely need to go through several drafts of your essay before it is ready for submissions. Once you are happy with the content of the essay, move on to the next two steps to prepare your essay for submission.
14. #### Edit your essay

    Once you have the content of the essay just the way you want it, edit your essay to improve style. You may want to review **Chapter 8**: “Edit: Improve *How* You’ve Written”(which was required reading in Unit 1).

    1. Complete“Checklist 8.1: Edit for Style.”
    2. If possible, work with a peer or a friend to complete “Practice 8.5”so that you can receive helpful feedback on your writing; then, edit again.
15. #### Create a list of sources

    Create a list of sources that catalogues every source you cited in your essay. Format it according to MLA or APA style.

    Use Purdue Owl’s [MLA](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/mla_style/mla_formatting_and_style_guide/mla_formatting_and_style_guide.html) or [APA](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/apa_style/apa_formatting_and_style_guide/reference_list_basic_rules.html) samples to ensure every entry is correctly done. Once on the page, look to the left at the Table of Contents, where you will find a section on periodicals, which is another name for journal articles. That is where you will find the samples you need. In addition, if you are using APA, as necessary, refer back to Unit 5, Learning Activity 8 and review the APA lecture. If you are using MLA, as necessary, refer back to Unit 5, Learning Activity 9 and review the Works Cited lecture.
16. #### Format and proofread your essay

    Finally, format and proofread your essay in preparation for submission. Give yourself plenty of time for this step. You might want to review **Chapter 9**: “Proofread: Polish Your Writing for an Audience” (which was required reading in Unit 3).

    - Proofread your essay and make corrections.
    - Complete “Checklist 9.1: Proofreading for Grammar and Mechanics.”
    - If possible, work with a peer or a friend to complete “Practice 9.3” so that you can receive helpful feedback on your writing. Make any remaining corrections.

    Double-check that you've used MLA style or APA style formatting correctly. Visit these links:

    ##### MLA

    1. [MLA General Format](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/mla_style/mla_formatting_and_style_guide/mla_general_format.html)
    2. [MLA Guide to Formatting a Paper (PDF)](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/mla_style/mla_formatting_and_style_guide/documents/20180702110400_747-2.pdf)

    ##### APA

    3. [APA General Format](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/apa_style/apa_formatting_and_style_guide/general_format.html)
    4. [APA Guide to Formatting a Paper (PDF)](https://apastyle.apa.org/style-grammar-guidelines/paper-format/student-annotated.pdf)
17. #### Prepare Assignment 6 for submission

    Proceed to the Assignment 6 checklist and review each item carefully. Make any necessary revisions and edits before submitting.

    > **Note:** PDFs of all articles must be submitted with the assignment. Tutors may ask for all paraphrases and quotations to be highlighted. Also note that tutors sometimes return assignments that are not done correctly to give students the best opportunity for learning and success.

### 49. Checklist for Assignment 6

After you have completed all of the required readings and followed all steps in Unit 6 to write your essay, use this checklist to evaluate whether your essay is ready for submission. If necessary, revise your essay before submitting it for marking.

1. The assignment is correctly formatted: headers, page numbers, margins, spacing, font, indentation, and alignment are correct, according to the guidelines of [MLA style](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/mla_style/mla_formatting_and_style_guide/mla_general_format.html) **or** [APA style](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/apa_style/apa_formatting_and_style_guide/general_format.html). I have compared the formatting of my assignment to the sample on *Purdue OWL.*
2. The assignment is structured as an essay of 1,000 – 1,200 words (excluding the list of sources).
3. The topic of the essay has been supplied by (or approved by) my tutor. The topic has been appropriately narrowed and is suitable for an argumentative essay.
4. The essay has an interesting title that is correctly formatted.
5. The introductory paragraph effectively introduces the issue/debate and includes a very brief summary of each side of the debate. This paragraph is not labeled with the heading “Introduction.”
6. The thesis/road map is clearly expressed in the last sentence of the first paragraph, which introduces the topic, the position, and the claims.
7. The thesis/road map statement does not include announcements such as “I will argue,” “I believe,” “This essay will argue,” or “My essay will prove.” If the thesis/road map statement contains such a phrase, revise it to remove this announcement.
8. The body paragraphs are arranged in the most logical order to prove the argument.
9. Each body paragraph is substantial and focuses on one distinct main idea that supports the thesis. The body paragraphs are **not** preceded by headings.
10. Each body paragraph begins with a topic sentence, includes at least two supporting points, and ends appropriately.
11. The topic sentences and closing sentences do not contain quotations or citations.
12. Each body paragraph contains relevant information from research that effectively supports the main idea of the paragraph and—by extension—the thesis.
13. The essay includes direct quotations, not just paraphrases.
14. Each piece of information from research is introduced and integrated effectively.
15. The essay contains transitional words.
16. The essay uses third-person point of view consistently throughout the essay.
17. Noting there are two approaches to conclusions,
    1. according to my tutor’s advice, the concluding paragraph emphasizes the thesis and very briefly sums up the main points, without repeating the thesis statement word for word (exhaustive).
    2. according to my tutor’s advice, the concluding paragraph is suggestive, so it reinforces the thesis without repeating it and **does not** sum up the main points. Rather, it evaluates, discusses implications, calls for action, provides a warning or prediction, or something similar (suggestive).
    3. the concluding paragraph is not labeled with the heading “Conclusion.”
18. The essay contains information from no less than four and **no more** than six research sources.
19. Every research source is reputable, reliable, and relevant.
20. At least three of the sources are from peer-reviewed scholarly journals.
21. There is a citation in each sentence that contains information from research sources.
22. Each citation is correctly formatted and matches the corresponding entry on the list of sources. Remember: the first word of the citation must match the first word of the corresponding entry.
23. The essay does not contain plagiarism—I have double-checked!
24. The list of sources is titled Works Cited (MLA style) or **References** (APA style).
25. The list of sources includes all the sources used in the essay, and each entry is formatted correctly. I have checked the format of each bibliographic entry against an [MLA sample](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/mla_style/mla_formatting_and_style_guide/mla_works_cited_page_basic_format.html) or an [APA sample](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/apa_style/apa_formatting_and_style_guide/reference_list_basic_rules.html).
26. I have revised the essay to improve coherence and unity.
27. I have edited the essay for style and clarity.
28. I have consistently maintained the third-person point of view throughout the essay.
29. I have proofread the assignment: grammar and mechanics (spelling, punctuation, capitalization, and format) are correct.
30. The essay is saved as a Microsoft Word file and the articles are saved in PDF format. I have named each article with the last name of the first author.
