>    - COMP101_Assignment1_DoeJane_1234567
>    - COMP101_Assignment1_file1_DoeJane_1234567
>    - COMP101_FinalAssignment_DoeJane_1234567



## 20 Common Errors


### 53. 20 Common Errors

Click the headings for more information.

#### 1. Sentence Fragment

A sentence fragment is—as the name suggests—a fragment or a piece of a sentence that does not form a complete correct sentence on its own.

There are two common kinds of sentence fragments, one that can result from a missing subject or a missing conjugated verb, and another that occurs when a group of words does not convey a complete thought.

Note: As you read this section, you will find it helpful to have open Chapter 24 of [Read, Think, Write](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=74852). The first two sections, “Components of a Sentence” and “Fragments,” explain terminology such as **subject**, **verb**, **dependent clause**, and **independent clause**.

##### The Missing Subject or Conjugated Verb

Sometimes, a subject and a verb are present, but the words do not express a complete thought.

Consider the group of words below. It contains a subject (George) and a verb (travelled), but it does not express a complete thought. Thus, it is a sentence fragment:

“And George travelled abroad.”

The main idea of the sentence is not complete. What happened before George travelled abroad? It is not clear.

The presence of “And” at the beginning makes this group of words a dependent clause. To understand the main idea, a reader would need more information so, in grammatical terms, the clause is dependent on the presence of an independent clause.

To fix the sentence fragment, add an independent clause:

“Marta worked for the summer, and George travelled abroad.”

Tip: *And* is a coordinating conjunction, one of seven conjunctions that can connect two independent clauses. The acronym FANBOYS helps you remember the coordinating conjunctions: *for*, *and*, *nor*, *but*, *or*, *yet*, *so*.

Here is another example. The group of words below does contain a subject (George) and a verb (found). However, *although,* the subordinating conjunction, makes the clause dependent. Thus, this is a sentence fragment:

“Although George found his wallet.”

To fix the sentence fragment, add an independent clause:

“Although George found his wallet, the money was gone.”

The main subject and the main verb of a sentence always appear in the independent clause, which carries the most important information in the sentence.

For more detailed information about sentence fragments, independent clauses, dependent clauses, subjects, and verbs, refer to Chapter 24 in [Read, Think, Write](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=74852).

To check your understanding of identifying subjects and verbs, [complete these exercises](https://skylinecollege.edu/learningcenter/assets/documents/grammarguides/ReaderIdentifyingSubjectsVerbs.pdf).

To check your understanding of independent and dependent clauses, complete the exercises on the [“Sentence Clauses”](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl_exercises/sentence_structure/sentence_clauses/index.html)  page of the Purdue OWL.

To check your understanding of sentence fragments, complete the exercises on the [“Sentence Fragments”](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl_exercises/sentence_structure/sentence_fragments/index.html)  page of the Purdue OWL.

#### 2 & 3. Fused Sentences & Comma Splices

As you read this section, you will find it helpful to have open [Chapter 24](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=74852) of *Read, Think, Write*. The sections on run-on sentences and comma splices explain the terminology used below and provide additional examples.

Fused sentences and comma splices occur when two sentences are incorrectly joined together. **A fused sentence** occurs when two complete sentences are incorrectly joined with **no** punctuation at all, whereas **a** **comma splice** occurs when two complete sentences are incorrectly joined with a comma.

Here are four examples of fused sentences:

1. The audience agreed the movie was terrible they told all their friends to avoid it.
2. Passengers on the plane were upset they had to sit on the tarmac for three hours.
3. The party was supposed to end at midnight some people stayed longer.
4. Sanjay never finished paneling his basement he hired a carpenter to complete the job.

Here are four examples of fused sentences. The only difference is the incorrect comma in between the sentences, which turns them into comma spliced sentences.

1. The audience agreed the movie was terrible, they told all their friends to avoid it.
2. Passengers on the plane were upset, they had to sit on the tarmac for three hours.
3. The party was supposed to end at midnight, some people stayed longer.
4. Sanjay never finished paneling his basement, he hired a carpenter to complete the job.

Although your goal is to create error-free sentences in the first place, during the editing stage, you may need to repair comma splices or fused sentences. You can do so with any of the following:

1. Using a period or semicolon between sentences
2. Using a comma followed by a joining word (and, but, or, so) or using a connecting word (although, after, since, because) without a comma
3. Using a period or semi-colon and then a transitional word followed by a comma

To know if you have written a fused sentence or a comma splice, check to see whether the sentence actually contains two (or more) complete sentences. Read the sections of the sentence to see if each can stand alone as a complete sentence (i.e., they are independent clauses). In the above examples, each of the clauses **could** stand alone as a complete sentence.

**The first** of three main ways to correct fused or comma spliced sentences is to insert a period or a semicolon to separate the complete sentences (independent clauses). Grammatically, it is equally correct to use a period or a semicolon. If the sentences are very closely related, a semicolon can emphasize this connection. If the sentences are not very closely related, a period would be better.

However, semicolons should be used sparingly and just for stylistic impact. Therefore, unless there is a particular reason to choose a semicolon, using a period would be preferable.

Here are some examples of repaired fused sentences and comma splices using method one.

1. The audience agreed the movie was terrible; they told all their friends to avoid it.
2. Passengers on the plane were upset. They had to sit on the tarmac for three hours.
3. The party was supposed to end at midnight; some people chose to stay longer.
4. Sanjay never finished paneling his basement. He hired a carpenter to complete the job.

**The second way** to correct a fused or comma spliced sentence is to add a comma and then a joining word (and, but, so, or) *or* add a connecting word without a comma (although, after, since, and many others). While variety is important in writing, a series of short simple sentences gives the impression of choppiness, so it is often more effective to consider this method.

Here are some examples of repaired fused sentences and comma splices using method two.

1. The audience agreed the movie was terrible, so they told all their friends to avoid it.
2. Passengers on the plane were upset since they had to sit on the tarmac for three hours.
3. The party was supposed to end at midnight, but some people chose to stay longer.
4. Sanjay never finished paneling his basement, so he hired a carpenter to complete the job.

**The third way** to correct a fused or comma spliced sentence is to add a period or a semi-colon and then a transitional word or phrase (examples: however, next, after, therefore, in addition, moreover, on the other hand, and many others).

Here are some examples of repaired fused sentences and comma splices using method three.

1. The audience agreed the movie was terrible; therefore, they told all their friends to avoid it.
2. Passengers on the plane were upset. Unfortunately, they had to sit on the tarmac for three hours.
3. The party was supposed to end at midnight. However, some people chose to stay longer.
4. Sanjay never finished paneling his basement. Instead, he hired a carpenter to complete the job.

For more detailed information about fused sentences and comma splices, independent clauses, dependent clauses, subjects, and connecting words, refer to Chapter 24 in [Read, Think, Write](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=74852).

To check your understanding of fused sentences and comma splices, complete the exercises on the [“Sentence Structure”](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl_exercises/sentence_structure/sentence_structure/index.html)  page of the Purdue OWL.

For more detailed information about fused splices, independent clauses, dependent clauses, subjects, and connecting words, refer to Chapter 24 in [Read, Think, Write](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=74852).

To check your understanding of fused (run-on) sentences, complete the exercises on the [“Sentence Structure”](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl_exercises/sentence_structure/sentence_structure/index.html)  page of the Purdue OWL.

#### 4. Dangling Participle

Dangling participles can create confusion—and sometimes unintended humour. A participle “dangles” when it does not match the noun it is supposed to describe or when it is placed so far away from its noun that the reader struggles to make the connection.

**Dangling Participle Comment and Corrections**

| Dangling Participle | Comment | Corrected Sentence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sitting in my lawn chair, the moose surprised me. | *The moose is sitting in the lawn chair?* | When I was sitting in my lawn chair, the moose surprised me. |
| Having fallen from the tree, Luis was startled by the beetle. | *Luis fell from the tree?* | Having fallen from the tree, the beetle startled Luis. |
| Growing up, my father baked the best biscuits for me. | *While the father was growing up, he baked biscuits for his child?* | When I was growing up, my father baked the best biscuits for me. |
| Soaked by the rain, the umbrella was no help. | *The umbrella was soaked by the rain?* | Because Michel was soaked by the rain, the umbrella was no help. |
| Beaten by the all-star team, the baseball game was over. | *The baseball game was beaten?* | The Royals were beaten by the all-star team, and the baseball game was over. |
| With the inclusion of graphics, the reader can understand the article. | *“With the inclusion of graphics” seems to describe the reader, which does not make sense.* | The author’s inclusion of graphics helps the reader to understand the article. |

For more detailed information about dangling participles, refer to Chapter 24 in *Read, Think, Write*.

#### 5. Misplaced Modifier

A modifier is a word or phrase that describes a noun or verb. In a sentence, the modifier should be placed near the noun it modifies. If the modifier is placed near a different noun, the reader will be confused.

**Misplaced Modifier Explanation and Correction**

| Misplaced Modifier | Explanation | Corrected |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The announcer called Tyrone **with a loud voice**. | *Because “with a loud voice” is placed next to “Tyrone,” it seems to describe Tyrone.* | The announcer **with the loud** voice called Tyrone. |
| The three friends sat at a corner table **sipping tea**. | *Because “sipping tea” is placed next to “a table,” it suggests that the table is drinking tea.* | The three friends **sipping tea** sat at a corner table. |
| Lise drank a **hot** cup of tea. | *Because “hot” is placed next to “cup,” it suggests that the cup, not the tea, is hot.* | Lise drank a cup of **hot** tea. |
| Roger encountered an eagle **on the way to school**. | *This sentence seems to suggest that the eagle was on its way to school.* | **On the way to school,** Roger encountered an eagle. |
| Natalia **nearly** studied for four hours. | *This sentence implies that for four hours, Natalia almost studied, but she did not actually study at all.* | Natalia studied for **nearly** four hours. |

For more detailed information about misplaced modifiers, refer to Chapter 24 in *Read, Think, Write*.

#### 6. Verb Tense Error

The most common verb tense errors have to do with a lack of consistency, usually from one sentence to another, but sometimes within a single sentence. When you edit your essays, be sure to check for consistent verb tense.

**Verb Tense Errors and Corrections**

| Verb Tense Error | Correct Verb Tense |
| --- | --- |
| We **were** driving through Innisfail when suddenly a funnel cloud **forms**. | We **were** driving through Innisfail when suddenly a funnel cloud **formed**. |
| My father **was** a kind man and **is** a role model. | My father **is** a kind man and **is** a role model.  or  My father **was** a kind man and **was** a role model. |

Another verb tense error, in a summary or a literary analysis, is using the past tense to to describe the content of the text. Always use the present tense. An example of how to do this correctly is:

- In “The Ways of Meeting Oppression,” Martin Luther King Jr. **argues** in favour of nonviolent resistance to oppression.

For more detailed information about verb tense, refer to Chapter 24 in *Read, Think, Write*.

To check your understanding of verb tense consistency, complete the exercises on the [“Tense Consistency”](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl_exercises/grammar_exercises/tense_consistency/index.html)  page of the Purdue OWL.

#### 7. Subject-Verb Agreement Error

Subjects and verbs should agree in number. If the subject of a sentence is singular (one person or one thing), the verb should be singular. If the subject is plural (two or more people or two or more things), the verb should be plural too.

##### Singular subjects require singular verbs

Here is a sentence with an agreement error:

- **The study**, which involves ten teachers and three hundred students, **are** scheduled to begin in July.

Although there are many participants, there is only one study, and *study* is the subject of the sentence.

The sentence might seem confusing at first glance, because it contains an interrupting phrase: “which involves ten teachers and three hundred students.” However, the interrupting phrase is not part of the essential grammar of the sentence; it does not contain the subject (the study) or the verb (to be).

To check that the subject and the verb agree, ignore the interrupting phrase, like this:

- **The study** which involves ten teachers and three hundred students **are** scheduled to begin in July.
- The **study are** scheduled to begin in July.

Now it is clear that the subject and verb do not agree. Here is the corrected sentence:

- **The study**, which involves ten teachers and three hundred students, **is** scheduled to begin in July.

##### Collective nouns

Collective nouns indicate a single group that is made up of multiple people, such as *a team*, *a group*, *a government*, *a choir*, *a family*, *a committee*. Because the group is singular, the verb should be singular too.

**Agreement Errors and Corrections**

| Agreement Error | Error Corrected |
| --- | --- |
| **The government are** responsible for those policies. | **The** **government is** responsible for those policies. |
| **The team are** poised to win. | **The team is** poised to win. |
| **My family like** to celebrate. | **My family likes** to celebrate. |

##### Plural subjects require plural verbs

When a sentence has two or more subjects, a plural verb is required. The sentence below has two subjects—*determination* and *perseverance*—so a plural verb is required.

**Agreement Errors and Corrections**

| Agreement Error | Corrected |
| --- | --- |
| **Determination and perseverance helps** me succeed. | **Determination and perseverance help** me succeed. |
| **A bike**, **a skateboard**, **and a scooter is** my primary **mode** of transport. | **A bike**, **a skateboard**, **and a scooter are** my primary **modes** of transport. |

For more detailed information about subject-verb agreement and collective nouns, refer to Chapter 24 in [Read, Think, Write](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=74852).

To check your understanding of subject-verb agreement, complete the exercises on the [“Subject-Verb Agreement”](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl_exercises/sentence_structure/subject_verb_agreement/index.html)  page of the Purdue OWL.

#### 8. Pronoun Agreement Error

Traditionally, singular pronouns were used to refer to singular people or things, and plural pronouns were used to refer to plural people or things. In the sentences below, *Alex* is **one** person (singular), while *students* refers to **more than one** student (plural).

- **Alex** [*singular*] wrote the exam, and **he** passed.
- **The students [*plural*]** wrote **their** exams in an hour.

However, both MLA and APA style guides now endorse usage of *they/them* to refer to a specific individual who prefers those specific pronouns over the binary male or female pronouns for reasons of inclusivity. Only use gender inclusive pronouns when applicable. Wherever possible, choose plural nouns/pronouns instead.

Here is an example of a gender inclusive sentence:

- **Alex** wrote the exam, and **they** passed.

However, as the *Chicago Manual of Style* suggests, in cases in which the singular *they/them/their* referring to an unspecified individual might make the meaning of the sentence ambiguous or confusing, the best option is to rephrase the sentence to avoid using a singular pronoun at all. For example, here is the sentence above reworded to avoid the need for a pronoun:

- **Alex** wrote and passed the exam.

Do **not** use plural pronouns *they/them/their* to refer to non-gendered singular nouns.

**Plural and Singular Pronouns**

| Incorrect | Correct |
| --- | --- |
| The board of directors reversed **their** policy. (There is only one board.) | The board of directors reversed **its** policy. |
| The team won, and **they** are going to the finals. (There is only one team.) | The team won, and **it** is going to the finals. |

For more detailed information about pronouns and collective nouns, refer to the sections “Gender-Biased Language” in Chapter 23 and “Pronoun Agreement” in Chapter 24 in [Read, Think, Write](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=74852), and complete Practice 24.14.

#### 9. Pronoun Reference Error

A **pronoun** is used to replace a noun (a person, thing, or concept).

- Michelle walked **her** dog. (*her* refers to Michelle)
- The Scouts set up **their** tents. (*their* refers to the Scouts)
- The dog wagged **its** tail. (*its* refers to the dog)

Sometimes, though, a reader has trouble figuring out what or whom a pronoun is supposed to refer to.

##### First-person pronouns

In informal speech, we often use the first-person pronoun *we* to refer to “people in general.” In formal writing, though, this can create confusion. Unless you have specifically defined the group that *we* refers to, the reader will not know who is included in the group. (Does *we* include the writer? The reader? Who else?) Choose more specific nouns.

**First-person Pronouns**

| Unclear Reference | Clear |
| --- | --- |
| **We** need to do more about climate change. | - **Legislators** need to do more about climate change. - **Citizens** need to do more about climate change. - **Scientists** need to do more about climate change. |

Avoid using the second-person pronouns *we* and *us* to refer to “people in general.”

##### Second-person pronouns

Likewise, do not use the second-person pronoun *you* to refer to “people in general.” Instead, choose specific nouns and third-person pronouns.

**Second-person Pronouns**

| Unclear Reference | Clear |
| --- | --- |
| If **you** want to be a famous actor, **you** should be willing to give up **your** privacy. | - If **one** wants to be a famous actor, **one** should be willing to give up **one’s** privacy. - **People** who want to become famous actors should be willing to give up **their** privacy. |

The second-person point of view can have the effect of confronting or accusing the reader in an uncomfortable way. Imagine, for example, reading the following sentences in an essay about safe injection sites.

**Second-person Point of View**

| Unclear Reference | Clear |
| --- | --- |
| If **you** are addicted to heroin, **you** should seek help. | **People who are addicted to drugs** can seek help. |

Therefore, the use of second-person point of view is discouraged in academic writing unless it is chosen with intention for a particular reason, such as in a how-to essay.

##### Third-person pronouns

In academic writing, use primarily third-person pronouns. To avoid confusing the reader, make sure it is clear what or whom each pronoun refers to.

**Third-person Pronouns**

| Unclear Reference | Problem | Clear |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Michelle told Diane that **her** flight was delayed. | (*Whose flight was delayed?*) | Michelle told Diane that **Diane’s** flight was delayed. |
| At the hospital, **they** told Trey to return in two days. | (*Who told Trey?*) | At the hospital, **the nurse** told Trey to return in two days. |
| The report and the Timbits are on the table. **This** is very important. | (*What is very important: the report or the Timbits?*) | **This repor**t is very important. |
| The invasion of Ukraine and the resulting war have created several problems. **It** is serious. | (*What is serious: the invasion, the war, or one of the problems*?) | **The problems** are very serious. |

#### 10. Pronoun Case Error

The role of a pronoun in a sentence—as either the subject of the sentence or the object of a sentence—determines its case.

##### Subject Pronouns

The subject of a sentence is the person doing the action. Subject pronouns are *I*, *we*, *he*, *she*, *it*, *they*, *who*, *whoever*.

Use *I* to refer to a person in the subject position (the person doing the action in the sentence).

**Subject Pronoun Error and Correction**

| Incorrect | Correct |
| --- | --- |
| **Kal and me** went to the movie. | **Kal and I** went to the movie. |
| To check whether *me* or *I* is correct in the sentence above, take Kal out of the sentence for a moment. | |
| **Me** went to the movie. | **I** went to the movie. |
| Who is going to the movie? *I* am going to the movie. Since *I* is correct, *I* is the correct choice, even when Kal is brought back into the sentence. | |

When writing from the third-person point of view, use *he*, *she*, or *they* to refer to people in the subject position.

**Subject Position Errors and Corrections**

| Incorrect | Correct |
| --- | --- |
| **Her and Alysha** went to the movie. | **She and Alysha** went to the movie. |
| To check whether *she* or *her* is correct in the sentence above, take Alysa out of the sentence for a moment. | |
| **Her** went to the movie. | **She** went to the movie. |
| Who is going to the movie? *She* is going to the movie. Since *she* is correct, *she* is the correct choice, even when Alysha is brought back into the sentence. | |

The pronouns *who* and *whoever* are used in the subject position when the subject of the sentence is unknown.

**Table Caption**

| **Incorrect** | **Correct** |
| --- | --- |
| **Whom** is going to the movie with Kal? | **Who** is going to the movie with Kal? |
| **Whomever** wants to come should get in the car now! | **Whoever** wants to come should get in the car now! |

##### Object pronouns

The object of a sentence is the person or thing receiving the action. Object pronouns are *me*, *us*, *him*, *her*, *it*, *them*, *whom*, *whomever*. Use *me* to refer to a person in the object position (the person receiving the action in the sentence).

**Object Pronouns Errors and Corrections**

| Incorrect | Correct |
| --- | --- |
| Kal bought a ticket for Cohen and **I**. | Kal bought a ticket for Cohen and **me**. |
| To check whether *me* or *I* is correct in the sentence above, take Cohen out of the sentence for a moment. | |
| Kal bought a ticket for **I**. | Kal bought a ticket for **me**. |
| *Me* is the correct choice, even when Cohen is brought back into the sentence. | |

When writing from the third-person point of view, use *him*, *her*, or *them* to refer to people in the object position.

**Third-person Errors and Corrections**

| **Incorrect** | **Correct** |
| --- | --- |
| Kal bought a ticket for Cohen and **she**. | Kal bought a ticket for Cohen and **her**. |
| To check whether *she* or *her* is correct in the sentence above, take Cohen out of the sentence for a moment. | |
| Kal bought a ticket for **she**. | Kal bought a ticket for **her**. |
| *Her* is the correct choice even when Cohen is brought back into the sentence. | |

The pronouns *whom* and *whomever* are used in the object position when the object of the sentence is unknown.

**Whom and Whomever**

| Incorrect | Correct |
| --- | --- |
| For **who** did Kal buy a ticket? | For **whom** did Kay buy a ticket? |
| I’ll buy a ticket for **whoever** Kal forgot. | I’ll buy a ticket for **whomever** Kal forgot. |

##### Reflexive pronouns

A reflexive pronoun is used when the same person (or thing) is both the subject *and* the object of the sentence. Reflexive pronouns are *myself*, *himself*, *herself*,*ourselves*, *themselves*, *itself*.

The following sentence is correct:

- **The cat** licked **itself**.

The cat is both the doer and the receiver of the action.

In the following, the subject and object are not the same entity. Therefore, a reflexive pronoun cannot be used.

**Reflexive Pronoun: Error and Correction**

| Incorrect | Correct |
| --- | --- |
| Bill, please read the report to **myself**. | Bill, please read the report to **me**. |

For more detailed information about pronoun case and reflexive pronouns, refer to the section “Subject and Object Pronouns” in Chapter 24 of [Read, Think, Write.](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=74852)

#### 11. Misused Colon

In a sentence, a colon can be used to introduce a list, a reason, a question, a quotation, or a single word. The words that follow a colon (i.e., the words that appear on the right side of a colon) do not need to form a complete sentence.

However, the words that come before the colon (i.e., the words that appear on the left side of a colon) must create an independent clause. If the words that come before the colon cannot stand alone as a complete sentence, the colon is incorrect.

One of the most common errors with colons is to place the colon midway through an independent clause, thereby creating a sentence fragment in the first part of the sentence.

**Misused Colon: Errors and Corrections**

| Incorrect | Sentence Fragment | Correct |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I need to buy: a birthday cake, candles, and decorations. | *I need to buy.* (The verb *buy* requires an object to make the clause complete). | I need to buy the following items: a birthday cake, candles, and decorations. |
| Please bring: a pencil, a notebook, and an eraser. | *Please bring.* (The verb *bring* requires an object to make the clause complete). | Please bring the following items: a pencil, a notebook, and an eraser. |

The phrase “the following” is often used to help with the challenge of ensuring that there is an independent clause before the colon. “The following” works as an object to make the clause complete.

For more detailed information about colons, refer to Chapter 25 in [Read, Think, Write.](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=74852)

#### 12. Misused Semicolon

The most common use of a semicolon is to connect two related independent clauses (i.e., two complete sentences). In this case, in terms of grammar, the semicolon functions exactly like a period does. Where you could not use a period, do not use a semicolon.

The difference between the period and the semicolon lies in meaning: the semicolon implies a closer relationship between two sentences than a period does.

For a semicolon to be correct, there must be independent clauses on *both* sides of the semicolon. In other words, if the words on either side of the semicolon could not stand alone as a complete sentence, the semicolon is incorrect.

One of the most common errors with semicolons is to place the semicolon between an independent clause and sentence fragment.

**Misused Semicolon: Errors and Corrections**

| Incorrect | Correct |
| --- | --- |
| Many Canadians singers found global success; particularly Celine Dion. | - Many Canadians singers found global success, particularly Celine Dion. - Many Canadians singers found global success; this was particularly true of Celine Dion. |
| Lightfoot stayed in Toronto; but Mitchell and Ste. Marie moved to New York. | - Lightfoot stayed in Toronto, but Mitchell and Ste. Marie moved to New York. - Lightfoot stayed in Toronto; Mitchell and Ste. Marie moved to New York. |

> **[Note]**
>
> **Tip:** There is a glitch in Microsoft Word’s grammar algorithm, and it will often suggest a semicolon when a semicolon would actually create a sentence fragment. Ensure that you understand the principles of correctly using semicolons so that you are not led astray.

For more detailed information about semicolons, refer to Chapter 25 in [Read, Think, Write](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=74852).

#### 13. Misused or Missing Comma

Do place a comma after an introductory word, phrase, or clause.

**Comma Use: Errors and Corrections**

| Incorrect | Correct |
| --- | --- |
| **However** you shouldclean your room first. | **However,** you should clean your room first. |
| **On Tuesday** I will fly to China. | **On Tuesday,** I will fly to China. |
| **If you are going to drive** don’t forget your driver’s licence. | **If you are going to drive,** don’t forget your driver’s licence. |

Do insert a comma between two independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction (the coordinating conjunctions are *for, and, nor, but, or, yet,* and *so—*easily remembered with the acronym FANBOYS).

**Commas and Coordinating Conjunction**

| Incorrect | Correct |
| --- | --- |
| Brad Pitt is the lead actor **and** Quentin Tarantino is the director. | Brad Pitt is the lead actor**, and** Quentin Tarantino is the director. |

Do enclose a parenthetical or interrupting expression in commas. This expression might consist of one word or a longer phrase.

**Enclose Parenthetical Expressions: Errors and Corrections**

| Incorrect | Correct |
| --- | --- |
| Sascha **however** was late. | Sascha**, however,** was late. |
| Be sure **of course** to take your driver’s licence. | Be sure**, of course,** to take your driver’s licence. |
| The reason for my absence **without going into too much detail** was a family emergency. | The reason for my absence**, without going into too much detail,** was a family emergency. |

Do *not* place a single comma between a subject and its verb. In the following sentence, *Moni* is the subject, and *travelled* is the verb. A single comma should not be placed between the subject and verb.

**No Comma Between Subject and Verb**

| Incorrect | Correct |
| --- | --- |
| **Moni** and her cat and dog, **travelled** to New Brunswick. | **Moni** and her cat and dog **travelled** to New Brunswick. |

Do *not* place a single comma between a verb and its object.

**No Comma Between Verb and Object**

| Incorrect | Correct |
| --- | --- |
| Mohammed likes to **play** baseball, and **volleyball**. | Mohammed likes to **play** baseball and **volleyball**. |

For more detailed information about commas, refer to Chapter 25 in *Read, Think, Write*. To check your understanding of commas, complete the exercises on the [“Commas”](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl_exercises/punctuation_exercises/commas/index.html)  page of the Purdue OWL.

#### 14. Misused or Missing Apostrophe

Do use apostrophes with singular and plural nouns to indicate possession.

 If a noun is singular (e.g., one *student*), add an apostrophe + *s*.

**Singular possession:** The **student’s** essay was about climate changes.

In this case, there is one essay belonging to one student, so the noun (*student*) is singular. The apostrophe is placed immediately after the word *student*, and an *s* is added.

If a noun is plural (e.g., several *students*), add an apostrophe **after** the *s*.

**Plural possession:** All of the **students’** essays were returned the next day.

In this case, there are many essays belonging to many students, so the noun (*students*) is plural. The apostrophe is placed immediately after the word *students*.

Do not use apostrophes with the possessive pronouns *its* and *whose*. *It’s* is a contraction that means “it is.” *Its* is a possessive pronoun.

**Apostrophes and Possessive Pronouns**

| Incorrect | Correct |
| --- | --- |
| **Its** frustrating that the government reversed **it’s** policy. | **It’s** frustrating that the government reversed **its** policy. |
| If you are not sure whether to use *its* or *it’s*, replace the word with “it is” and listen to see if it sounds correct or not. The error will become apparent. If it sounds correct, choose *it’*s; if not, choose *its*. | |
| **It is** frustrating that the government reversed **it is** policy. | **It’s** frustrating that the government reversed **its** policy. |

*Who’s* is a contraction that means “who is.” *Whose* is a possessive pronoun.

**Who's and Whose**

| Incorrect | Correct |
| --- | --- |
| **Whose** coming to the movie with me, and **who’s** car shall we take? | **Who’s** coming to the movie with me, and **whose** car shall we take? |
| If you are not sure whether to use *whose* or *who’s*, replace the word with “who is” and listen to see if it sounds correct or not. The error will become apparent. If it sounds correct, choose *who’s*; if not, choose *whose*. | |
| **Who is** coming to the movie with me, and **who is** car shall we take? | **Who’s** coming to the movie with me, and **whose** car shall we take? |

Do not use apostrophes to make a noun plural.

**Apostrophes and Plural Nouns**

| Incorrect | Correct |
| --- | --- |
| The professor returned the essays to the **student’s**. | The professor returned the essays to the **students**. |
| the **1960’s** saw an explosion in folk music. | the **1960s** saw an explosion in folk music. |

For more detailed information about apostrophes, refer to Chapter 25 in [*Read, Think, Write*](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=74852). To check your understanding of apostrophes, complete the exercise on the [“Apostrophes”](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl_exercises/punctuation_exercises/apostrophes/index.html)  page of the Purdue OWL.

#### 15. Parallelism

When you are presenting ideas that are parallel, use parallel grammatical form. If one item in the list is in a different form, the writing becomes awkward.

##### Parallel Parts of Speech

**Parallel Parts of Speech**

| Non-Parallel Structure | Parallel Structure |
| --- | --- |
| That teacher is **passionate** [adjective], **dedicated** [adjective], and **inspires** her [verb] students. | That teacher is **passionate** [adjective], **dedicated** [adjective], and **inspiring** [adjective]. |
| She inspires **confidence** [noun], **respect** [noun], and **the students cooperate** [independent clause]. | She inspires **confidence** [noun]**, respect** [noun], and **cooperation** [noun]. |

##### Parallel Verb Form

**Parallel Verb Form**

| Non-Parallel Structure | Parallel Structure |
| --- | --- |
| I love t**o write**, **to read**, and **knitting**. | I love **to write**, **to read**, and **to knit**. |
| Would you prefer **to walk** or **drive**? | Would you prefer **to walk** or **to drive**? |
| Pierre **drove** to the park and **walks** his dog. | Pierre **drove** to the park and **walked** his dog. |

##### Parallel Comparisons

**Parallel Comparisons**

| Non-Parallel Structure | Parallel Structure |
| --- | --- |
| He prefers **the green socks** to the **socks that are brown**. | He prefers **the green socks** to the **brown socks**. |
| It’s easier to **hike down** a hill than **hiking up a hill**. | It’s easier to **hike down** a hill than to **hike up****.** |
| **Snowboarding** is as easy to learn as **to learn how to ski**. | **Snowboarding** is as easy to learn as **skiing** is. |

To learn more about parallelism, visit the [“Parallel Structure”](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/mechanics/parallel_structure.html)  page of the Purdue OWL.

#### 16. Mixed Construction

Mixed construction occurs when the elements of a sentence do not match, grammatically or logically. Mixed construction often confuses the reader, who must struggle to figure out how the parts of the sentence work together.

**Mixed Construction**

| Mixed Construction | The Problem | Revised |
| --- | --- | --- |
| These statistics propose that more research is needed. | *How can statistics propose something?* | An analysis of the statistics reveals that more research is needed. |
| The most valued trait in a nurse is a person who is compassionate. | *How can a person be a trait?* | The most valued trait in a nurse is compassion. |
| The author’s serious and repetitive tone conveys urgency. | *How can a tone be repetitive?* | The author’s serious tone, together with his use of repetition, conveys urgency. |
| For a practical nurse to become an RN it requires the bridging program. |  | A practical nurse who wants to become an RN should take the bridging program. |
| Arachnophobia is when you are extremely afraid of spiders. |  | Arachnophobia is an extreme fear of spiders. |
| The reason I like horror movies is because they make me feel scared. |  | I like horror movies because I like to feel scared. |

To learn more about mixed construction, visit the [“Mixed Sentence Constructions”](https://openstax.org/books/writing-guide/pages/9-6-editing-focus-mixed-sentence-constructions)  page of Rice University’s Writing Guide and TCK Publishing’s [“Mixed Constructions: What They Are and How to Avoid Them”](https://www.tckpublishing.com/mixed-constructions/)  page.

#### 17. Overuse of Passive Voice

A typical sentence is structured like this: subject + verb + object. This structure is called *active voice*. In *passive voice*, the order of the key grammatical elements is reversed.

**Active Voice** — Subject [S] Verb [V] Object [O]

**Passive Voice** — Object [O] Verb [V] Subject [S]

Look closely at the examples to note the positions of the subject (the girl), the verb (kicked), and the object (the ball).

Active Voice — **The girl** [S] **kicked** [V] **the ball** [O].

Passive Voice — **The ball** [O] was **kicked** [V] by **the girl** [S].

> **[Note]**
>
> Notice that because the order of the subject and the object are reversed in the passive voice, the sentence requires two additions: the verb *to be* (*is*, *are*, *was*, *were*) and the word *by*.

There are three particular circumstances in which passive voice is a good choice:

1. **The subject is unknown**

   **Passive Voice** — The jewels were stolen!

   **Active Voice** — Someone stole the jewels!

   In this case, the identity of the thief is unknown, and the focus of the sentence is the action (stealing) and the object (jewels). Therefore, passive voice is a good choice.
2. **The subject is obvious**

   **Passive Voice** — The thief was arrested.

   **Active Voice** — The police arrested the thief.

   In this case, the subject of the sentence (police) is implied, and the focus of the sentence is the action (arresting) and the object (thief). Therefore, passive voice is a good choice.
3. **The subject is unimportant or irrelevant**

   **Passive Voice** — two compounds were mixed together.

   **Active Voice** — The scientist mixed together the two compounds.

   In this case, the subject of the sentence (the particular scientist) is unimportant, and the focus of the sentence is the action (mixing) and the object (two compounds). Therefore, passive voice is a good choice.

For these three reasons, passive voice is often used in journalism and in scientific reports.

However, in other circumstances, passive voice can be a poor choice, especially if it is overused. Passive voice creates two stylistic problems: *wordiness* and *lack of clarity*.

**Wordiness:** Because passive voice requires the addition of the verb *to be* and the preposition *by*, it is wordier than active voice.

**Lack of Clarity:** Because passive voice often omits the subject of the sentence, the reader can become confused about who is doing what.

**Passive and Active Voice**

| Voice | Example | Comment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Passive Voice** | The new regulations were implemented. | (unclear subject) |
| **Passive Voice** | The new regulations were implemented by the CEO. | (clear but wordy) |
| **Active Voice** | The CEO implemented the new regulations. | (clear and concise) |

Unless there is a good reason to choose passive voice, choose active voice instead.

For more detailed information about the parts of a sentence, refer to Chapter 24 in [Read, Think, Write](https://drr2.lib.athabascau.ca/index.php?c=node&m=detail&n=74852) .

#### 18. Overuse of the Verb **To Be**

The verb to be has several forms: *is*, *am*, *are*, *was*, *were*, *be*, *being*, *been*. The verb *to be* is essential to the English language and is often necessary in a sentence. However, when overused, the verb *to be* can contribute to a lack of clarity and a lack of specificity because it is often used in place of more precise verbs. It can also lead to wordiness.

| **Wordy** | **It is** carbon dioxide **that is** trapping heat in the atmosphere. |
| --- | --- |
| Not only does the verb *is* appear twice, unnecessarily, but the structure of the sentence requires extra words (*it* and *that*), which contribute to wordiness. Also, the main verb (*trap*) is buried as the third verb in the sentence, rather than taking centre stage, where it belongs. | |
| **Concise** | Carbon dioxide **traps** heat in the atmosphere. |

Look at another example:

| **Wordy** | **There are** many environmental problems **that are** requiring immediate action. |
| --- | --- |
| Again, the verb *are* appears twice in the sentence. Also, the structure requires the extra words *there* and *that*. The main verb (*require*) is buried as the third verb in the sentence. | |
| **Concise** | Many environmental problems **require** immediate action. |

For more detailed information about the reasons for avoiding the overuse of *to be*, visit the [“Avoid Common Pitfalls”](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/academic_writing/conciseness/avoid_common_pitfalls.html)  page of the Purdue OWL and the [“Active Voice and ‘Be’ Verbs”](https://louisville.edu/writingcenter/for-students-1/handouts-and-resources/handouts-1/active-voice-and-be-verbs)  handout from the University of Louisville Writing Centre.

#### 19. Misuse of **Which/That** and **Who/Whom** and **Where**

##### *That* or *Which*?

*That* is used with restrictive clauses. A **restrictive clause** is a clause that contains information that is essential to the sentence because that information identifies a particular entity.

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Restrictive Clause | The Canadian law **that legalizes cannabis** was passed in 2018. |

In the example above, because there are many Canadian laws, the restrictive clause is essential to identifying which particular law the sentence is about. The restrictive clause begins with *that.* The restrictive clause is not set off with commas.

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Non-Restrictive Clause | The *Cannabis Act*, **which came into effect in 2018,** legalized cannabis. |

In the example above, the sentence already identifies the particular law: the *Cannabis Act*. The fact that the law came into effect in 2018 is extra information; it is not essential to identifying the particular law. Therefore, the clause is **non-restrictive.** The non-restrictive clause begins with *which,* and it is set off with a comma.

##### *That/Which* or *Who*?

Use *who* to refer to **people**. Use *that/whic*h to refer to **things**.

**People**

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Restrictive Clause | The man **who** is wearing a red hat is my uncle. |
| Non-Restrictive Clause | My Uncle Joe, **who** is wearing a red hat, is visiting. |

**Things**

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Restrictive Clause | The bill **that** the Liberals introduced was passed. |
| Non-Restrictive | The *Cannabis Act*, **which** came into effect in 2018, legalized the sale and use of cannabis. |

##### Misuse of Where

A writing habit that has crossed over from informal speech is the use of *where* to replace the words *that*, *which*, and *when*.

Do not use *where* to refer to time periods, conditions, or situations.

**Misuse of Where**

| Incorrect | Correct |
| --- | --- |
| Did you read **where** the prime minister is speaking in Iqaluit? | Did you read **that** the prime minister is speaking in Iqaluit? |
| The 1980s were a decade **where** big hair ruled. | The 1980s were a decade **when** big hair ruled. |
| Cases **where** a physician wasn’t available increased by half. | Cases **in which** a physician wasn’t available increased by half. |

Do use *where* to refer to places.

**Correct Use of Where**

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Correct | Quebec City is the place **where** Beth would like to get married. |

To learn more about relative pronouns, visit the [“Introduction and General Usage in Defining Clauses”](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/grammar/relative_pronouns/index.html)  page and the [“That vs. Which”](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/grammar/that_vs_which.html)  page of the Purdue OWL.

#### 20. Problems in Attributive Tags

An **attributive tag** is a phrase that precedes a quotation or a piece of information from research. It tells your reader where you found the quotation or the information, and it gives the author credit for it. An attributive tag includes the author’s name and a verb such as “states” or “writes.” Here is an example:

**Jenkins states** that carbon dioxide traps heat in the atmosphere.

Many verbs can be used in attributive tags.

##### Verbs that Introduce Quotations or Information from Research

admits, affirms, argues, articulates, asserts, claims, clarifies, concedes, concludes, contends, conveys, describes, discusses, emphasizes, highlights, identifies, illustrates, implies, insists, maintains, mentions, notes, observes, outlines, points out, posits, proposes, proves, recognizes, recommends, refutes, rejects, remarks, reminds, reports, shows, suggests, theorizes, urges, warns, writes

Some common problems occur in students’ use of attributive tags.

##### Not Choosing the Verb Carefully

Many times, students do not give a lot of thought to which verb they choose from the above list. However, each verb implies something specific about the relationship between the author, the author’s thesis, and the information in the sentence. Therefore, it is important to choose carefully. Otherwise, the effect may be jarring for the reader. For more information on choosing appropriate verbs that convey the meaning you intend, visit Newcastle University’s [“Reporting Verbs”](https://www.ncl.ac.uk/academic-skills-kit/writing/academic-writing/reporting-verbs/)  page.

##### Not Choosing Carefully Between How and That

In attributive tags, some of these verbs can be followed by either *how* or *that*. For example, both of the following sentences are grammatically correct.

###### Correct

Jenkins explains **that** carbon dioxide traps heat.

Jenkins explains **how** carbon dioxide traps heat.

Although both sentences are technically correct, do not make a careless choice between *how* and *that*. Carefully re-read the two sentences to examine the differences in meaning implied by the words *how* and *that*.

Jenkins explains **that** carbon dioxide traps heat.

In the first sentence, the choice of *that* tells the reader that Jenkins is making a **statement** that presents a fact: carbon dioxide traps heat.

Jenkins explains **how** carbon dioxide traps heat.

In the second sentence, the choice of *how* tells the reader that Jenkins is about to explain a **process**: the steps in the process of trapping heat. The reader will expect to learn *how* the process happens.

> **[Note]**
>
> Remember: If you use *that*, your reader will expect a statement. If you use *how*, your reader will expect a process. If you use *how* when *that* would be a better choice, your reader might be confused.

#### Using That and How Incorrectly

Some verbs can be followed by the word *that*, but not *how*, including *claims* and *states*.

**That and How**

| Incorrect | Correct |
| --- | --- |
| Jenkins states **how** . . . | Jenkins states **that** . . . |

#### Misusing Commas in Attributive Tags

If an attributive tag includes *that*, it should not include a comma—regardless of whether you are paraphrasing or quoting.

**Misusing Commas**

| Incorrect | Correct |
| --- | --- |
| Jenkins states that, carbon dioxide traps heat. | Jenkins states that carbon dioxide traps heat. |
| Jenkins states that, “carbon dioxide traps heat.” | Jenkins states that “carbon dioxide traps heat.” |
| However, if you are treating a quotation as dialogue, do include a comma, but do not include *that*. | |
| - | Jenkins states, “Carbon dioxide traps heat.” |

If you would like to learn more about these guidelines, search online for “that-complements and wh-complements with reporting verbs,” and you will find handy reference guides and articles showing how to pair verbs with *that*, *how*, or other words like *when*, *where*, *why*, and *what*.

## Final Exam


### 55. Final Exam

At the end of your course, you will write a three-hour supervised (invigilated) final exam to ensure that you have achieved the learning outcomes of the course. You may bring a dictionary with you (and it may combine English and another language if English is not your first language).

The final exam counts for 20% of your course mark, and you must achieve a mark of 50% or better on the exam to pass the course. If you do not pass the exam the first time, you may write one supplemental exam. See the Athabasca University Undergraduate Calendar for more information on [supplemental exams.](https://www.athabascau.ca/calendar/undergraduate/exams-grades/supplemental-exams.html)

The exam results and your final grade will be available to you approximately five business days after you write it. The exam will not be returned to you, but you will receive a brief note from your tutor with your results. Should you wish to appeal your exam grade, consult [Appeals](https://www.athabascau.ca/calendar/undergraduate/exams-grades/marks-and-grades.html#appeals)  in the online Athabasca University Undergraduate Calendar for more information.

This is an [online exam](https://www.athabascau.ca/support-services/exam-services-support/writing-online-exams.html) , and it will contain the following four sections:

#### Part A: Essay (50 marks)

Write a 500- to 600-word essay on your choice of four topics. The topics will be general enough to allow you to write based on your personal experience and knowledge. Your essay should demonstrate proficiency in one of the following modes of organization: process, classification, comparison, or cause-effect. Take time to create an outline or a plan, and be sure to focus the essay on a clear thesis. The essay should include the following:

- a title
- an introductory paragraph that includes a strong thesis statement
- two or three body paragraphs, each beginning with a topic sentence
- a concluding paragraph that sums up and restates the thesis

Set aside time for both planning and proofreading. The essay will be marked on content, organization, mechanics, grammar, and style.

Part A is worth 50% of the exam mark, so spend approximately 50% of your time (60 to 90 minutes) on it.

#### Part B: Summary (20 marks)

For Part B, you will read an unfamiliar article (provided with the exam). Then, you will write a one-paragraph summary of that article (approximately 150–200 words in length). Begin the paragraph with the article title, the author’s name, and a restatement of the author’s thesis. Then, follow the steps in “10 Steps to Writing a Successful Summary” (in Chapter 15 of *Read, Think Write*) to write a summary of the article.

Part B is worth 20% of the exam mark, and you will spend approximately 30 minutes on it.

#### Part C: Excerpt Analysis (10 Marks)

For Part C, you will need to be familiar with **one** of the essays listed below. Most likely, you will choose the essay you summarized for Assignment 2, but if you prefer, you may choose another.

- [“How to Write with Style”](https://kmh-lanl.hansonhub.com/pc-24-66-vonnegut.pdf)  by Kurt Vonnegut
- [“I Wrote the Super Queer Novel My Younger Self Needed”](https://electricliterature.com/would-i-have-realized-i-was-gay-sooner-if-queer-books-were-mainstream/)  by Celia Laskey
- [“Life Is Too Short for Someone Else’s Shame”](https://disabilityvisibilityproject.com/2020/09/16/life-is-too-short-for-someone-elses-shame/)  by Amanda Leduc
- [“No Place for Self-Pity, No Room for Fear”](https://www.thenation.com/article/archive/no-place-self-pity-no-room-fear/)  by Toni Morrison
- [“On Fighting for Space in the Literary World as a Black Canadian Writer”](https://lithub.com/on-fighting-for-space-in-the-literary-world-as-a-black-canadian-writer/)  by Cheryl Thompson
- [“On Keeping a Notebook”](https://sanmiguelwritersconference.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/10/406-706-Looking-Back-Moving-Forward-Jessica-Handler.pdf)  by Joan Didion
- [“Politics and the English Language”](https://www.orwellfoundation.com/the-orwell-foundation/orwell/essays-and-other-works/politics-and-the-english-language/)  by George Orwell
- [“Shitty First Drafts”](https://wrd.as.uky.edu/sites/default/files/1-Shitty%20First%20Drafts.pdf)  by Anne Lamott
- [“Why I Write”](https://www.nytimes.com/1976/12/05/archives/why-i-write-why-i-write.html)  by Joan Didion
- [“Why I Write”](https://www.orwellfoundation.com/the-orwell-foundation/orwell/essays-and-other-works/why-i-write/)  by George Orwell
- [“Why I Write Indigenous Sci-Fi”](https://canadianart.ca/essays/why-i-write-indigenous-sci-fi/)  by Drew Hayden Taylor
- [“Write Till You Drop”](https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/books/99/03/28/specials/dillard-drop.html)  by Annie Dillard

On the exam, you will see a list of twelve excerpts, one from each essay listed above. You will choose one excerpt to work with.

You will write a paragraph that a) identifies the essay title and the author, and b) examines the role and significance of the excerpt and how it functions in the article in relation to the author’s thesis. (See Preparing for the Final Examination, below, for more information.)

Part C is worth 10% of the final exam mark, and you will likely spend 20 to 30 minutes on it.

#### Part D: Grammar and Mechanics (20 marks)

Part D consists of 20 multiple-choice questions, each containing one of the errors included in “20 Common Errors” document at the end of the Study Guide, Activities, and Assessments. For example, a question might contain a comma splice, a sentence fragment, a semicolon error, a parallelism error, a dangling participle, etc. You do not need to be able to label/name the errors, but you do need to be able to identify a correct or incorrect sentence from a multiple-choice list.

Part D is worth 20% of the exam mark, and it will likely take only 15 to 20 minutes if you have prepared adequately.

#### Preparing for the Final Exam

1. Prepare for Part A.

   Review Chapters 12 and 16 in *Read, Think, Write*. Review your tutor’s feedback on Assignments 3 and 5.

   Practice writing an essay, from start to finish, within a time limit. Choose a topic from Practice 16.2, 16.3, 16.4, or 16.5 in *Read, Think, Write*. Give yourself 75 minutes to write the practice essay, from planning to proofreading.
2. Prepare for Part B.

   Review Chapter 15 in *Read, Think, Write*, paying particular attention to “10 Steps to Writing an Effective Summary” and “The Dos and Don’ts of Writing a Summary.” Review your tutor’s feedback on Assignment 2.

   Practice writing a summary. Choose one of the articles in Unit 2 that you have not already written about. Choose one page of the article to summarize. Give yourself 40 minutes to read the page and to write a summary.
3. Prepare for Part C.

   For Part C, you will work with **one** of 12 essays. Do not try to memorize all 12 essays. Do not even memorize one! You do not need to read any of the other essays listed for Part C **except** for the one you wish to work with.

   Shortly before the exam, review your notes from Learning Activity 5 in Unit 2. Re-read your chosen essay. Memorize the title and author. Read the essay closely, using the active reading strategies you learned in Unit 2. Write out a restatement of the author’s thesis, in your own words. Memorize it. Identify the main supporting points.

   To practice for Part C, choose an important sentence from your essay and pretend that it is the excerpt you see on the exam. Determine the role of excerpt:

   - Is it the author’s thesis statement?
   - Is it a key supporting idea?
   - Is it a main argument or a key reason?
   - Is it a piece of evidence?
   - Is it a supporting detail? If it is a supporting detail, is it a statistic, a fact, an example, an anecdote, etc?
   - Is it an analogy or a metaphor?
   - Does it appeal to logic or emotion?
   - Is it an introduction or a conclusion?
   - Does it have any other roles, such as establishing tone?

   Give yourself 20 minutes to write a paragraph that 1) identifies the title and author, 2) restates the article’s thesis, and 3) thoroughly explains the role of excerpt by answering the questions above.

   In the first sentence of your paragraph, identify the essay title and the author (“This excerpt is from . . . ). Then, paraphrase the author’s thesis.

   The rest of the paragraph should be devoted to identifying the role and significance of the quotation. How does the excerpt relate to the author’s thesis? What is the job of the quotation in supporting the thesis? Which specific words or phrases in the quotation demonstrate its role? In your paragraph, quote them and explain their significance.
4. Prepare for Part D.

   To prepare for Part D, review the “20 Common Errors” document at the end of the Study Guide, Activities, and Assessments, and study the examples. All 20 errors will be represented on the exam. Pay particular attention to the errors that your tutor has flagged in your assignments.

   > **Note:** You may take a dictionary into the exam, but you may not use any other books or sources.
5. On exam day, be as rested and relaxed as you can.

   We recommend, above all, that you have a good night’s rest and try to relax. This exam should have no surprises. We want to assess your essay-writing, summarizing, and critical thinking skills. We also want to see your ability with grammar and have assurance that the tone and style of your writing matches that of your previous course submissions. We do not expect your writing to be as polished as it might be if you had more time.
6. Manage the exam.

   1. Look the whole exam over once. This will calm your nerves and prepare you to write.
   > **Remember:** You have a maximum of three hours to complete the exam. Most students use the full three hours. Budget your time accordingly.

   2. Proceed to Part A, and choose the essay topic you would like to write about.
   3. Next, answer the following questions for yourself—and based on those answers, make a rough outline for the essay:

      - Who is my audience?
      - What is my purpose?
      - Therefore, what should be my style and type of writing (e.g., personal, expository, persuasive)?
      - What is my thesis?
      - What is the topic/topic sentence in each of my three or four body paragraphs?
      - What sort of supporting detail will I need to mention for each point made in each paragraph?

      Your essay should demonstrate a clear, sufficiently detailed thesis (usually placed at the end of your opening paragraph) and two or three solid body paragraphs of 6–12 sentences each. Use good paragraph craft so that each paragraph has focus, support, and a clear, effective relationship to your thesis. **Give yourself 90 minutes for planning and writing your essay.**
   4. Use your dictionary. Remember that you may bring a dictionary with you, and it may combine English and another language if English is not your first language. Use your dictionary initially just to check the precise meanings of any key words in the essay assignment instructions. Once you reach the essay-revision stage, use your dictionary to check spellings, if you have time.
   5. Manage your remaining time. Assuming you have used the full 90 minutes to prepare and write Part A, you will have 90 minutes left to complete your exam. We recommend using that time as follows:

      Part B: 40 minutes
      Part C: 20 minutes
      Part D: 20 minutes
      Final Revision: 10 minutes

      This timeline is just a recommendation. The important thing is to keep an eye on the clock so you do not spend too much time on any one section.
7. A few more tips

   - Do not waste time typing out exam instructions or essay topics. Instead, get straight to your answer.
   - While it is a good idea to jot notes or make an outline for your essay on a piece of paper, do not try to write out a complete first draft. If you do, you will likely run out of time and energy in your final draft.
   - You will have limited ability to format your answers in the exam software. You do not need to double-space. Instead of indenting, hit the return key twice and leave a blank line to indicate a paragraph break. Instead of italics for book or film titles, use quotation marks.
   - There is no spell-check in the exam software. Leave time to proofread.
   - You do not need to provide any in-text citations or bibliographies.
   - If you get stuck on a grammar question, guess, then move on. You can go back to it later if you have time. Each grammar question is worth only one mark, so do not waste time pondering an individual question. Your time is better spent proofreading your essay.

#### Requesting Your Exam

Remember that it is your responsibility to request your final exam. There are **strict deadlines for such requests**, so please visit the [Exam Services Support](https://www.athabascau.ca/support-services/exam-services-support/index.html)  website for important details.

Information and links for requesting exams are available on the [Exams and Grades](https://www.athabascau.ca/calendar/undergraduate/exams-grades/index.html)  page of the AU Undergraduate Calendar.

You can also fax your request to 780–675–6174 or send your request by mail to:
